issues.title: config_node.rs declared_base() is a second Rust base resolver that falls back to current_dir()
issues.body:
LOOSE ENDS from the two-halves-one-node plan, from its only whole-plan review (the per-task gates were skipped on that plan and the review was scoped accordingly):

(a) packages/tractor/src/host/plugin_host/config_node.rs:48-55's `declared_base()` is a SECOND Rust base resolver and still falls back to current_dir(). The guarantee holds only because run_daemon sets SOVEREIGN_BASE in-process first -- and it skips doing so when refarm_dir.parent() is None.

CLOSED 2026-08-12 with the operator's section 8 authorisation. Both halves this item names, plus a
third the second half was hiding.

(a) THE cwd FALLBACK IS GONE. It had been NAMED earlier the same day (`DeclaredBaseOrigin::Cwd`),
which was an improvement and not a fix: the TypeScript resolver has no fifth step, so on a machine
where nothing above answers the two implementations returned DIFFERENT bases and the node rooted
itself in whatever directory a shell last `cd`-ed to. `resolve_declared_base` returns `Option` now
and ends exactly where the TS chain ends. The impure edge PANICS, naming all four things it asked
-- a node that cannot resolve its base cannot function, and refusing is better than operating out
of an invented one.

(b) THE DAEMON NO LONGER SKIPS SETTING SOVEREIGN_BASE. It used `if let Some(base) =
refarm_dir.parent()`, and `Path::new("/").parent()` is `None` -- so a sovereign dir at the
filesystem root left the variable unset and every later read fell through the chain. It settles
through `dirname_like_ts` now, the same helper the resolver uses, which answers `/` for `/` exactly
as `path.dirname()` does.

(c) FOUND WHILE FIXING (b), AND WORSE: the node descriptor was published with
`PathBuf::from(std::env::var("SOVEREIGN_BASE").unwrap_or_default())`. With the variable unset that
is an EMPTY PATH, published as this node's base -- a descriptor stating a wrong answer as a fact,
which is worse than one that says nothing. It publishes the base the node actually resolved.

PARITY PROVEN IN BOTH LANGUAGES, for the inputs ISS-028 named:

    REFARM_HOME=.refarm      Rust "."       TS "."
    REFARM_HOME=/            Rust "/"       TS "/"
    REFARM_HOME=/x/.refarm   Rust "/x"      TS "/x"

`Path::parent()` agrees with NEITHER on its own -- it answers `Some("")` and `None` -- which is why
`dirname_like_ts` exists and why the daemon had to use it too.

  tractor 1482 lib tests, 18 in config_node (3 new, one per half)
issues.resolved_by: the cwd step removed and the daemon's SOVEREIGN_BASE settled through dirname semantics, 2026-08-12

issues.title: --refarm-dir has no TypeScript counterpart, so the base guarantee is scoped to env-declared nodes
issues.body:
LOOSE ENDS from the two-halves-one-node plan:

(c) `--refarm-dir` has no TypeScript counterpart: a node started with `--refarm-dir /srv/x/.refarm` and no env exports settles /srv/x, while the CLI answers $HOME, so the guarantee is scoped to env-declared nodes and is currently stated unconditionally.

DECIDED 2026-08-10 — SCOPE THE CLAIM, DO NOT MIRROR THE FLAG. Two ways to close this and only one of them is honest at this size:

Mirroring the flag means every CLI command grows a `--refarm-dir` and threads it through every resolver, because a base passed to one command and not another is worse than no flag at all. That is the centralisation slice (one resolved node scope, injected end to end), not a patch — and until it exists, a half-mirrored flag would make the two halves disagree in a NEW way while appearing to fix the old one.

What actually holds today, measured: `run_daemon` sets SOVEREIGN_BASE in-process from `--refarm-dir` before any config-node code runs, so the DAEMON and everything it spawns are consistent. A CLI invoked separately, in a shell without those exports, is a different process and cannot know what flag the daemon was started with. That is not a bug in the CLI; it is the boundary between two processes, and the honest form is to say so rather than to imply a guarantee that spans it.

So this item closes as a SCOPING correction: the guarantee is stated for env-declared nodes, and `refarm context` already reports which of SOVEREIGN_BASE / REFARM_HOME / home answered (cliBaseOrigin, now derived from declaredBaseWithOrigin rather than a mirrored ternary — ISS-025). An operator on a --refarm-dir node sees `home` there and can tell. The flag mirror is folded into the centralisation slice, where it costs one field instead of thirty.

issues.title: The budget re-query is unbounded on a hot path — UsageRecord is never reaped
issues.body:
LOOSE ENDS QUEUE, opened at the operator's request on 2026-08-06:

(2) The budget re-query is unbounded and on a hot path: query-nodes filters by node TYPE not by
provider, and node_reap.rs's REAPABLE_TYPES omits UsageRecord so it is never pruned, so
system-wide volume drives it and once tripped the full fetch is a permanent per-call cost. Ways
out: host-side summing, or a provider-scoped query.

MEASURED 2026-08-11, on the operator's live node (~/.refarm/data/refarm/default.db, 276 KB):

     73  SessionEntry
     73  TaskEvent
     37  Task
     37  UserPrompt
     36  UsageRecord      <- this item's subject
     30  BudgetObservation
     10  Session

THE RE-QUERY DOES NOT FIRE TODAY, and cannot until this grows by three orders of magnitude. It
exists only for a TRUNCATED first read, and the first read asks for 10,000. Thirty-six rows do
not truncate. The "permanent per-call cost" the item describes is real in structure and has
never been paid.

That reframes the work rather than closing it. The growth is unbounded and the cost is a cliff,
not a slope: nothing degrades until the day the first read truncates, and from then on every
call pays a full fetch. But building for it now would be building for 36 rows.

THE OBVIOUS FIX IS THE WRONG ONE. Adding UsageRecord to REAPABLE_TYPES deletes SPEND HISTORY —
the exact rows the budget guard sums, and the rows `refarm budget observations` reports from.
node_reap.rs's own header states the rule that forbids it: a type "enters the allowlist only
alongside a live consumer, sized to that consumer's poll horizon". UsageRecord's live consumer
is the budget window (WINDOW_30D_NS in packages/agent/src/session/wasm_ops.rs), so a TTL here
would have to be comfortably beyond 30 days AND would still be destroying the operator's own
record of what he spent. That is a data-retention decision about his money, not a cleanup.

THE TWO REAL WAYS OUT, both needing a query-contract change (packages/plugin-wit):
  - PROVIDER-SCOPED QUERY. `query_nodes` filters by type only; a filter that also took a
    provider (and ideally a since-timestamp, since the window is 30 days) would make the read
    proportional to what the guard actually needs instead of to everything the node has ever
    recorded.
  - HOST-SIDE SUMMING. The host computes the windowed sum and returns a number. Smallest wire,
    largest behaviour change, and it moves arithmetic the agent currently owns and tests.

The since-timestamp is the more valuable half of the first option: the budget's question is
"spend in the last 30 days", and today it fetches all of history to answer it.

TRIGGER TO REVISIT, so this does not sit here as an opinion: when UsageRecord passes ~2,000 rows
on any real node, or when a first read is ever observed truncating. Re-run the count with the
query above.

VISIBLE HALF CLOSED 2026-08-11. `refarm budget observations|by-*|usage` now emit `completeness`
(complete|partial|unknown) beside `summary` on every --json surface, and the human notice derives
from the same shared judgement. The sums were already computed over a page that may have been cut;
what was missing was the sums SAYING SO to a consumer deciding "under budget".

The hot-path half is untouched and still gated on the same trigger recorded above: the re-query
cannot fire until UsageRecord volume grows ~3 orders of magnitude past the 36 rows measured on the
operator's live node.

## TRIGGER RE-RUN 2026-08-23 -- still gated, and now with a rate

     163  SessionEntry        163  TaskEvent          82  Task
      82  UserPrompt           81  UsageRecord <-      75  BudgetObservation
      32  Session

36 rows on 2026-08-11, 81 on 2026-08-23: ~3.75/day over twelve days, on a node that spent 33 of
those hours dead. The trigger is 2,000 and the first read asks for 10,000, so at this rate the
re-query cannot fire for well over a year. Building for it now would still be building for 81 rows.

WHAT CHANGED AROUND IT, and it is why this was re-measured rather than assumed: the node was set to
`runtime.autostart always` on 2026-08-23 and now runs continuously instead of when a terminal asks.
The rate above therefore UNDERSTATES what a daily-driver node will produce. The trigger stands; the
next re-run should compare against 81 rather than 36, and expect a steeper line.

issues.title: queryNodes returns a bare list, so eight consumers cannot tell a page from a table
issues.body:
RE-MEASURED 2026-08-10, and the item's first claim is STALE while its second turns out to be the root of the whole family.

STALE: 'packages/sidecar-client reads only body.nodes and DISCARDS stored/truncated'. It does not. packages/sidecar-client/src/index.ts:141-148 reads both, refuses to default `truncated` to false or derive `stored` from nodes.length, and carries a doc comment stating the three-state rule. Fixed at some point after this item was filed on 2026-08-06.

STILL TRUE, AND LARGER THAN IT LOOKS: 'eight call sites still discard truncated'. They discard it because THE CONTRACT HAS NOWHERE TO PUT IT. packages/storage-contract-v1/src/types.ts:59 declares `queryNodes(type: string): Promise<unknown[]>` -- a bare list. Every consumer of that interface (tractor-ts, storage-node-view, barn's plugin ledger, farmhand, me-runtime, skill-capability, tractor-store) is STRUCTURALLY unable to know whether it received a page or the whole table. It is not eight independent oversights; it is one missing field, eight times.

MEASURED SHAPE: 17 call sites across 8 implementations of `queryNodes` -- farmhand, tractor-store, sidecar-client, storage-node-view, storage-rest, storage-sqlite, sync-loro, and the tractor-ts mock adapters. The sidecar-client is the ONE that already carries the fields, because it speaks HTTP and the HTTP body has them; the contract below it does not.

THIS ITEM IS THE ROOT OF GROUP F. ISS-044 (farmhand re-sorts Sessions by created_at_ns) cannot be closed before it: sorting the whole list and slicing is correct ONLY while the page is complete, and there is no way to check completeness through a contract that cannot express it. ISS-042 (no paging past MAX_NODES_PER_RESPONSE) and ISS-047 (the WIT returns a bare list<string>, the same silent ceiling one layer lower) are the same missing field at the HTTP and WASM boundaries.

SO IT IS A SLICE, NOT A FIX, and it needs its own spec and plan the way the ledger and probe slices did: change the contract to carry {rows, stored?, truncated?}, migrate 8 implementations, then let ISS-042/044/047 close against it with a fixture larger than each limit. Sizing it as a quick fix is how it would land half-done -- which is the state it is in now.

CONTRACT LANDED 2026-08-11 (spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-11-a-page-says-it-is-a-page-design.md,
steps 2-4). The root is closed; the migration deliberately is not.

WHAT SHIPPED, and the count that matters is that NOTHING was forced to guess:

  packages/storage-contract-v1
    QueryNodesPage { nodes, stored?, truncated? }   both facts optional, absent means absent
    readCompleteness(page) -> complete | partial | unknown       ONE judgement, was four
    StorageAdapter.queryNodesPage?(type, options?)               OPTIONAL, and that is the design
    auditPageCoherence / runQueryNodesPageConformance            the conformance the spec named

  packages/sidecar-client
    QueryGraphNodesResult now EXTENDS QueryNodesPage instead of restating it. The rule was written
    here first and lived here alone; two declarations that agree today can drift tomorrow, and
    extending turns that into a compile error. QueryGraphNodesOptions became an alias, because an
    interface that adds nothing is a second declaration pretending to be a first (the linter said
    so before the reviewer could).

  apps/refarm/src/commands/budget.ts
    the human notice branches on readCompleteness rather than on the raw field, and all three
    --json surfaces carry `completeness` beside the sums it qualifies.

WHY queryNodesPage IS OPTIONAL, since it will read as a hedge to whoever finds it next: fifteen
files implement StorageAdapter. A REQUIRED method makes every one of them invent truncated:false
-- the single value that must never be guessed. `queryNodesPage === undefined` is itself the third
state, in the type system: THIS ADAPTER CANNOT TELL YOU. Same idiom as Effort.workspace_source
riding beside workspace_id rather than replacing it.

STILL OPEN: no storage adapter implements queryNodesPage yet, and the 19 consumers still call the
bare queryNodes. They are not broken and no deadline forces them; each adopts when it has a reason.
The conformance is what makes adoption checkable rather than trusted -- an adapter that implements
the method and reports truncated:false while stored exceeds nodes.length FAILS it, which is the one
lie the type cannot prevent.

THE TWO CONSUMERS THE SPEC NAMED AS HAVING A REASON: one did, one does not. Measured 2026-08-12 so
nobody builds the second.

  apps/refarm/src/commands/budget.ts   REAL, and adopted. It reads GET /nodes over HTTP, where
                                      MAX_NODES_PER_RESPONSE caps at 100, and it SUMS what it
                                      reads. Done in the same slice as the contract.

  packages/barn/src/index.ts           NOT a reason. `listPlugins()` calls `PluginLedger.queryNodes`,
                                      and `PluginLedger` is barn's OWN interface with NO implementor
                                      anywhere in this repository outside its tests — so there is no
                                      truncating backend behind it. The operator's node has ONE
                                      plugin. Adopting the page there would be building for a risk
                                      that does not exist, which is the shape ISS-039 already named
                                      ("building for it now would be building for 36 rows").

ALSO CHECKED AND CORRECT ALREADY: `apps/refarm/src/utils/tractor-store.ts`'s
`tractorGraphFromNodeView` synthesises `stored: nodes.length, truncated: false`. That looks like the
invented-completeness shape this family exists to stop, and it is not: `NodeView.queryNodes` reads
every row of the type in one pass with no ceiling, so both values are correct BY CONSTRUCTION. Its
own comment already says so, at length.

SO THE REMAINING MIGRATION IS NOT A BACKLOG OF 19. It is: whichever consumer next reads a paged
HTTP surface and cares whether it got everything. There is no such consumer today that is not
already adopted.

issues.title: GET /tasks holds an unlimited query, a second sort order and a silent truncate
issues.body:
CONFIRMED 2026-08-11, and there is a FOURTH defect nobody filed.

  sidecar/mod.rs:1732  storage.query_nodes("Task")            unlimited — materialises the table
  sidecar/mod.rs:1760  tasks.sort_by(created_at_ns DESC)      a second sort order
  sidecar/mod.rs:1766  tasks.truncate(limit.min(100))         silent truncate
  sidecar/mod.rs:1768  { tasks, total: tasks.len() }          <- THE FOURTH

`total` is computed AFTER the truncate, so it always equals the page size. A consumer reading
`total` to ask "is there more?" is answered "no", always. That is not a missing signal, it is a
wrong one — worse than the absent `stored`/`truncated` the item already names.

ALSO MEASURED: `get_task`'s fallback path does another unlimited `query_nodes("Task")` to do a
`contains` match on the id, and the status/session_id filters run AFTER the limit — the same
global-limit-then-filter shape ISS-045 just fixed in the agent, where it made an older task report
zero events.

Design, with the four changes and why removing `total` is safer than redefining it:
docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-11-a-page-says-it-is-a-page-design.md (step 5).

packages/tractor is a CLAUDE.md section 8 protected surface.

CLOSED 2026-08-11. All four defects fixed in packages/tractor/src/sidecar/mod.rs::get_tasks, and
the fourth was never filed by anybody: `total` was computed AFTER the truncate, so it always
equalled the page size and answered "no" to every "is there more". REMOVED rather than redefined --
a key whose meaning changes silently is worse than one that vanishes loudly, and nothing outside
this file's own tests read it (measured before removing).

The filters moved into SQL WITH the limit, never behind it. Moving only the limit would have been
worse than leaving the endpoint alone: `?status=done` would answer out of the newest 100 rows of any
status and could report zero while hundreds of done tasks existed -- ISS-045's shape, rebuilt in the
act of fixing something else. `stored` is counted over the same predicate, so `truncated` compares
two numbers measured over one set. That coupling is now structural: `count_nodes_matching` takes the
page's own spec rather than a copy of its filters, after a first draft that copied only the filters
and disagreed with the page whenever no filter was passed.

The endpoint also gained `offset`, because these fixes give it a `truncated` and a `truncated: true`
with no way to reach the rest is the complaint ISS-042 already is.

NOT CLOSED BY THIS, and now filed as ISS-115: `GET /tasks` orders by `created_at_ns` while the
guest's `list_tasks` orders by the store's `updated_at`. The plan said to drop the created_at sort,
which would make them agree -- and would silently change what `refarm tasks` MEANS, and make it
disagree with farmhand's TS sibling. The real defect is that neither surface says which question it
answers.

issues.title: No paging past MAX_NODES_PER_RESPONSE — rows beyond 100 are unreachable at any limit
issues.body:
LOOSE ENDS QUEUE, opened at the operator's request on 2026-08-06 -- obvious fixes to be resolved definitively rather than decided one at a time. Each is named with its file so none needs rediscovering:

(5) No paging past MAX_NODES_PER_RESPONSE -- rows beyond it are unreachable at any limit.

ALSO RECORDED, in a second handoff entry that named the same thing:

Deferred from the record-reader plan, triaged, each its own ticket:

(c) there is no paging past MAX_NODES_PER_RESPONSE, so rows beyond 100 are unreachable at any limit and the response does not say so;

RE-MEASURED 2026-08-11 and CONFIRMED: NodesQuery carries `type` and `limit` and nothing else -- no
offset, no cursor. The contract half is now in place (ISS-040): QueryNodesPage has somewhere to put
the page facts, and readCompleteness is the shared verdict. What remains is the transport, and it
is spec step 6 -- `offset` on GET /nodes, in packages/tractor, a CLAUDE.md section 8 surface. Not a
cursor: cursors need a stable sort key no adapter guarantees today, and
docs/SOVEREIGN_RECORD_ORDERING.md is the document that would have to change first.

CLOSED 2026-08-11. `GET /nodes` and `GET /tasks` accept `offset`, echo it back, and
`NativeStorage::query_nodes_page` applies it in SQL. `MAX_NODES_PER_RESPONSE` STAYS -- the fix is
reachability, not removal of the ceiling.

`truncated` had to change meaning to make paging honest: it is `stored > offset + nodes.len()`, not
`stored > nodes.len()`. Rows before the offset were skipped on purpose and are reachable by asking
again; counting them as withheld would leave a caller paging forever, one empty page at a time. The
last page of a truncated read reports `truncated: false` even though `stored` still exceeds what it
carries. Pinned by its own test.

NOT A CURSOR, and the docs say so rather than implying otherwise: a cursor needs a sort key stable
under concurrent writes, which no adapter guarantees and docs/SOVEREIGN_RECORD_ORDERING.md would
have to settle first.

REACHED THE OPERATOR, which is the half that would otherwise have been invisible: `refarm budget
observations|by-*|usage` and `refarm tasks` all take `--offset`, and their truncation notices now
name the command and the number that reaches the rest. That notice had been WRONG TWICE in opposite
directions -- first "raise --limit" (which could not work), then "not reachable today" (true when
written, false the moment offset shipped) -- so it now names a runnable command, which is the only
form of the claim that goes stale loudly.

issues.title: Diagram drift is ungated: CI disables strictness explicitly and the local browser is unpinned
issues.body:
LOOSE ENDS QUEUE, opened at the operator's request on 2026-08-06 -- obvious fixes to be resolved definitively rather than decided one at a time. Each is named with its file so none needs rediscovering:

(9) Diagram drift is ungated everywhere: local now computes and can fail, CI disables strictness explicitly. Root cause is SVG output not being reproducible across browser versions. Order: pin the browser locally as CI does, verify byte-stability, THEN decide about CI -- that last step is the operator's, it can break the pipeline.

ALSO RECORDED, in a second handoff entry that named the same thing:

DIAGRAM DRIFT IS UNGATED, and the operator has a decision to make. Verified: the CI workflow sets REFARM_DIAGRAM_SYNC_STRICT=0, which check-diagrams.mjs:137-139 treats as advisory -- it warns and returns before process.exit(1). So drift fails nothing in CI, and before 2026-08-06 it was not even computed locally. `diagrams:check` now runs --ci with no baked override, so it computes and CAN fail; on this machine it exits 1 on ~35 SVGs because the local browser differs from the one CI pins via scripts/ci/install-puppeteer-browser.mjs. That failure is genuine drift genuinely observed. ORDER OF OPERATIONS: pin the same browser locally FIRST, verify byte-stability, and only then decide whether CI should stop being advisory. That last part is the operator's call, not an agent's -- it could break the pipeline.

RE-MEASURED 2026-08-12, AND THE ROOT CAUSE NAMED IN THIS ITEM IS WRONG. It says "SVG output not
being reproducible across browser versions" and orders the work as "pin the browser locally as CI
does, verify byte-stability, THEN decide about CI". The first step is already done and does not
help.

FOUR MEASUREMENTS, in the order that settles it:

1. THE BROWSER IS ALREADY PINNED AND INSTALLED HERE. `install-puppeteer-browser.mjs --dry-run`
   resolves `chrome-headless-shell@148.0.7778.97`, and ~/.cache/puppeteer holds exactly that
   version. CI runs the same installer. Local and CI render with the same binary.

2. `diagrams:check` STILL FAILS on 10 SVGs.

3. THE RENDER IS DETERMINISTIC WITHIN A MACHINE. Rendering twice back to back produced 15 of 15
   BYTE-IDENTICAL files. So it is not nondeterminism, and it is not the browser.

   (A first attempt to test this was WRONG and nearly published: `diagrams:check` detects drift with
   `git status --porcelain`, so running it after `diagrams:fix` compares the tree to HEAD and always
   reports drift. It measures the working tree, not the renderer. The honest test renders twice and
   compares the two outputs to each other.)

4. THE FONT IS DECLARED AND NOT PROVIDED. `specs/diagrams/mermaid.config.json` asks for
   `'IBM Plex Sans', 'Segoe UI', sans-serif`. `fc-list | grep -i "IBM Plex Sans"` returns ZERO on
   this machine, so the renderer falls back to whatever fontconfig calls sans-serif — and every text
   width moves with it. The diff is exactly that shape: `max-width: 2466.81px` -> `2314.33px`, a 6%
   layout shift across 1057 differing regions, not a rounding difference.

SO THE CONFIG ALREADY WENT FOR DETERMINISM -- `deterministicIds: true`, a fixed `deterministicIDSeed`,
a pinned browser -- and left ONE non-deterministic input: a font named rather than supplied.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY FIX IT, and the choice is still the operator's:
  (a) SUPPLY THE FONT. `@fontsource/ibm-plex-sans` is OFL-1.1, 2.4 MB unpacked, and mermaid-cli
      takes `--cssFile`, so an `@font-face` pointing at the vendored file makes every renderer use
      the same glyphs. This is the only option that makes the bytes stable across machines.
  (b) Change `fontFamily` to something every environment resolves identically -- which nothing
      reliably is, since fontconfig differs per distro.
  (c) Leave CI advisory, and accept that the SVGs in git are one machine's rendering.

THE ORDER IN THIS ITEM SHOULD BE REPLACED: pinning the browser is done and was never the lever.
Supply the font, verify byte-stability across this machine and CI, THEN decide about
REFARM_DIAGRAM_SYNC_STRICT -- and that last step is still the operator's, because turning it on can
break the pipeline.

OPTION (a) WAS ATTEMPTED 2026-08-12 AND DOES NOT WORK. Recorded in full so nobody spends the same
afternoon on it.

THE ATTEMPT: add `@fontsource/ibm-plex-sans` (OFL-1.1), write a stylesheet with `@font-face` for
weights 400 and 600, and pass it to mermaid-cli with `--cssFile` (documented as "CSS file for the
page").

FAILURE 1, silent: the first version used an absolute `file://` URL for the font. Nothing changed
at all -- the page mermaid-cli renders is itself a `file://` document, and Chrome refuses a font
subresource across that boundary without `--allow-file-access-from-files`. The run REPORTED
SUCCESS and re-rendered every diagram in the fallback face.

FAILURE 2, the decisive one: embedding the font as a base64 `data:` URI removed the origin problem
and STILL changed no layout. The proof is in the output -- `data-flow.svg` grew from 37 KB to
99 KB (the embedded font is in there, `@font-face` appears twice) while `max-width` stayed at
2314.33px, the exact fallback figure. So `--cssFile` content reaches the OUTPUT SVG, after mermaid
has already measured the text. CSS that arrives after layout cannot change layout.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE REAL FIX: the font has to exist for the RENDERING PAGE at measurement
time, which means fontconfig, not CSS. And that needs a `.ttf`/`.otf` -- fontconfig does not read
woff2. Neither `@fontsource/ibm-plex-sans` nor `@ibm/plex-sans` ships one; both are web formats
only.

SO THE OPTIONS NARROW TO:
  (a') Vendor a TTF/OTF of IBM Plex Sans and point a repo-local `fonts.conf` at it via
       FONTCONFIG_FILE for the mmdc child process only -- no machine mutation, deterministic, and
       the font source has to come from somewhere other than these two packages.
  (b)  Change `fontFamily` to a family the render environment always has. DejaVu and Liberation
       are present here (34 faces) and are on essentially every Linux CI image, so this is more
       viable than it first looked -- at the cost of the diagrams' typography.
  (c)  Leave CI advisory and accept that the committed SVGs are one machine's rendering.

EVERYTHING FROM THE ATTEMPT WAS REVERTED: the dependency, the stylesheet, the `--cssFile` wiring
and the 43 regenerated SVGs. The working tree is exactly as it was.

CLOSED 2026-08-12 by changing the QUESTION rather than by pinning anything.

The three options this item and its re-diagnosis offered -- vendor a font, pick a font every
machine has, stay advisory -- all try to make the RENDER reproducible across machines. That
requires pinning the browser, the font, fontconfig and the renderer version, forever, and every pin
decays: the browser WAS pinned and identical to CI's, and it still drifted.

So the gate stopped asking the environment question and started asking the only one that is a
defect: IS THIS SVG DERIVED FROM THE CURRENT SOURCE?

    render:  generate, then append  <!-- refarm-diagram-source: sha256=... -->
    --ci:    read the recorded hash, recompute it, compare. No browser.
    --stamp: record it on what is already committed, WITHOUT re-rendering

THREE INPUTS TO THE HASH, each earning its place: the `.mermaid` source; `mermaid.config.json`,
because a theme edit redraws everything while no source moves; and the mermaid-cli VERSION, which
is the one real thing byte-comparison caught that a source hash would otherwise miss.

THREE STATES, not two: `current`, `stale` (source moved, SVG did not) and `unstamped` (predates
the gate). Both failures block and each prints its own remedy, because `--stamp` and `--fix` are
different repairs and telling somebody a never-stamped file is "stale" blames them for a lapse
that never happened.

MEASURED:
    verification   ~2 minutes (43 renders through headless Chrome)  ->  48 milliseconds
    migration      43 SVGs stamped, bodies BYTE-IDENTICAL to what was committed
    proof          a one-line edit to a .mermaid turns the gate red, names the file, prints --fix

The migration used `--stamp` precisely so the committed SVGs keep whatever machine rendered them.
Re-rendering to stamp would have replaced all 43 with THIS machine's fallback-font output -- the
environment-specific bytes the change exists to stop caring about.

WHAT IT NO LONGER CATCHES, stated plainly: a hand-edited SVG whose recorded hash still matches.
That is forgery rather than drift, and byte comparison never caught it either -- the forger would
have committed the bytes.

THE CI DECISION IS NOW TRIVIAL AND STILL THE OPERATOR'S. `REFARM_DIAGRAM_SYNC_STRICT=0` was set
because strictness could break the pipeline on an environmental difference. It cannot any more: the
gate reads files and reaches the same verdict everywhere. The workflow line can drop both the
`=0` and the `install-puppeteer-browser.mjs` that precedes it, since verification no longer needs a
browser.

THE CI LINE IS DONE TOO, 2026-08-12, at the operator's word (section 8 surface):

    - node scripts/ci/install-puppeteer-browser.mjs && REFARM_DIAGRAM_SYNC_STRICT=0 pnpm run diagrams:check
    + pnpm run diagrams:check

Strict, and no browser. The escape hatch existed because a byte comparison could fail on an
environmental difference — a font the runner lacked — and that cannot happen against a recorded
source hash.

A SECOND DEFECT THE HASH MADE VISIBLE, fixed in the same line-set: the workflow triggered only on
`**/*.mermaid`, and `specs/diagrams/mermaid.config.json` is now a HASH INPUT. A theme edit would
have made all 43 diagrams stale while running nothing at all. It is a trigger path on both the
pull_request and push filters now.

Left alone deliberately: `install-puppeteer-browser.mjs` and `puppeteer-no-sandbox.json` remain in
`validation-cache-files`. They no longer affect VERIFICATION, only re-rendering, so removing them
would change cache keys for no correctness gain — a wider edit than section 6 asks for.

Also not done, and worth someone's judgement later: `.svg` files are not trigger paths. Reverting
an SVG alone would go unnoticed until the next .mermaid edit. Widening the trigger is a real
improvement and a real increase in workflow runs; it is a separate decision from this one.

issues.title: The WASM bridge still materialises whole tables and its WIT returns a bare list with no truncation signal
issues.body:
RE-MEASURED 2026-08-11 against the code. BOTH HALVES OF THIS ITEM ARE STALE, and the reason is
worth recording: it was filed on 2026-08-06 against the state of the tree BEFORE that same day's
fix, and nothing re-read it since.

issues.title: The quota denominator: nothing records the operator's billing anchor or plan size, so 'how many left' is unanswerable
issues.body:
The fourth axis (quota). OPERATOR RULING 2026-08-12: THE DENOMINATOR IS NOT A DECLARATION, IT IS AN EXTRACTION. Extract from the access already granted; a provider that exposes nothing is a THIRD state; and then granularity BY WORKSPACE, allocating part of the quota to one workspace and part to another.

STEP 1 -- MEASURE WHAT EACH PROVIDER EXPOSES: DONE (ISS-129, closed as superseded 2026-08-18). `credential quota` reads github-copilot's per-meter entitlement/remaining/reset from `copilot_internal/user`; openai-codex answers `cannot-ask`, which is the third state arriving on its own rather than being defaulted to a guess.

STEP 2 -- THE SURFACE EXTRACTS RATHER THAN ASKS: DONE in spirit. `refarm credential quota` and `refarm budget quota` take "the accounts are configured" as the starting point and name what they could not extract. Nobody types a plan size.

STEP 3 -- WORKSPACE ALLOCATION: HALF DONE, and the halves are worth separating.

  SEEING (done, cf8bf2d9): `budget quota` shows which workspaces spent each seat, in the provider's own period, largest first. On the operator's node: rcdc5 -> pessoal, refarm -> corporativo. Dispatches naming no workspace get their own line rather than being diluted into a share.

  CAPPING (not done, and it needs a contract change): `BudgetAxis` is `deadlineMs | maxTokens | maxUsd`. The subscription meter counts REQUESTS regardless of size, so no token or dollar ceiling protects a shared seat -- one workspace can exhaust it without approaching any cap that exists. Adding a requests axis is cross-language: the TS contract in budget-contract-v1 (types, BUDGET_AXES, resolve) plus the Rust mirror in packages/tractor/src/sidecar/budget.rs and its callers in dispatch.rs and observation.rs, plus host enforcement.

  It now has a measured reason to weigh it against rather than a hypothetical: the operator's corporate seat went from 1706 remaining to 0 during the session that measured it. The three-level fold (node/workspace/declared) already exists and already binds -- this is the consumer it was built for.

A SECOND LIMIT ON CAPPING, worth stating before anyone builds it: refarm cannot bound the PROVIDER'S meter, because other clients spend it too. A requests ceiling governs what this node will dispatch on a workspace's behalf. That is useful and it is not the same as a share of the seat, and the surface must not let the two be confused.

  refarm project automations tick [--submit]        a host that ticks, on demand

the contract, echoed back in every job description, and READ BY NOTHING. A nightly job in
America/Sao_Paulo answered `declared` at midnight in Sao Paulo and `due` at nine in the evening,
while reporting the zone as if it had been honoured. Fixed the same day -- see the commit.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING, and it is one sentence: NOTHING CALLS THE TICK ON A CLOCK. Verified on
this node -- no systemd timer (only refarm-web-serve.service), no crontab, nothing in the repo, and
no periodic loop in the daemon. The executor is complete and unreached.

TWO WAYS TO CLOSE IT, and the choice is the operator's:
  (a) the daemon's own loop, which is spec D1 and packages/tractor (a section 8 surface). It is the
      right long-term home -- the daemon already holds the effort store, resolves budgets and
      writes observations, so an automation run costs nothing extra to govern.
  (b) a systemd user timer calling `refarm project automations tick --submit`. The node already
      runs exactly this arrangement for refarm-web-serve, it is reversible in one command, and it
      proves the whole path end to end before any Rust is written.

(b) is not a worse (a). It is how you find out whether the loop is the hard part before building
the hard part, and D5's missed-window reporting is easier to get right with a supervisor that
records its own misses.

The classic branch-protection endpoint still answers 404 "Branch not protected", which is what
this item was written from. That endpoint does not see RULESETS, and there is one:

issues.title: Should the budget record cover work refarm did not dispatch? ~6.5M subagent tokens are invisible to every query
issues.body:
OPERATOR RULING 2026-08-12: YES, the record should cover work this node did not dispatch -- and it must SEPARATE the two. Conditional on the provider giving it in a form that is easy to AUDIT.

SHIPPED 2026-08-18 in three commits (a4fba351, 6f5a861c, e21a8d37). The condition became satisfiable the same day: the Copilot quota reader built for ISS-129 exposes plan, sku, resetsAt and per-meter kind, and openai-codex answers cannot-ask -- the ruling's own third state arriving unprompted.

THE RULING'S MIDDLE FIGURE CANNOT BE COMPUTED, and finding out why was worth more than the figure. The provider meters PREMIUM INTERACTIONS while the record counts tokens and requests; the meters reset on a date, so an all-time dispatch count is the same units error moved into time; and the model dispatched that day landed on an unlimited meter while nothing recorded which meter a dispatch spends. So `consumed - dispatched` would assert an attribution nobody measured. A test exists whose only job is that the string `notDispatched` never appears in the output.

WHAT IT REPORTS INSTEAD: both numbers side by side, in the provider's own period, with the attribution between them named. Measured on the real node -- corporativo at 8294 of 10000 consumed, 1706 left, against 16 requests this node dispatched.

THE WINDOW is derived from the reset date and LABELLED derived-from-reset. A mid-month reset is refused rather than guessed: that could be monthly-from-signup or weekly, and a guess produces a window that looks measured. No window means the count is null, which is a different statement from the measured 0 an account with a known window and no traffic gets.

STEP 3 -- WHICH METER A DISPATCH SPENDS. Two cheaper answers were measured away: the provider does NOT say per dispatch (twelve response headers, none about quota), and a hardcoded model-to-meter table would age in silence. What is left is this node's own before/after measurement, declared with a DATE; an undated fact is dropped rather than trusted. Measured: gpt-4o on github-copilot moves neither premium meter.

Attribution has two values, and the missing third is deliberate: `none` is claimable when every model dispatched was measured not to touch the meter; a NUMBER is not, because this provider publishes per-model multipliers, so one dispatch is not one interaction.

WHAT REMAINS OPEN:
1. The per-model multiplier. Knowing a model spends the meter still does not say how much. Until that is measured or published in an auditable form, a metered row with a spending model stays `unknown` -- correctly.
2. 36 dispatches in the record name no account. They predate account attribution and are counted against nobody's quota, which is honest but is also a hole in the denominator.
3. `modelMeters` is written by hand today. Declaring it through the consent journey, the way `nodeTools` is, is a consistency question the operator has not been asked.

issues.title: Does the bench need a correctness axis richer than substring --expect?
issues.body:
Does the bench need a correctness axis richer than substring? `--expect` grades work whose answer is checkable that way and nothing else. An automation with a known expected result is a scenario WITH a grader, which is the cheap path; a judge model is the expensive one. Neither is built.

OPERATOR RULING 2026-08-12: the bench needs GRADUATION, not one more assertion type.

His words: bring in the axes that peers and the industry have found worth tracking, and let that
open the way to formulating our own -- and make it EASY to take what he does day to day and drop it
into the bench as an example to evaluate against.

That is two requirements, and the second is the load-bearing one:

1. ADOPT BEFORE INVENTING. Survey what is actually tracked (correctness, calibration, refusal
   behaviour, tool-use success, cost per solved task) and take the ones that fit, rather than
   designing an axis set from first principles. This repository's own standing preference is to
   assimilate a proven technique and cultivate the instrument, not to invent the metric.
2. THE INGESTION PATH IS THE FEATURE. A bench nobody feeds measures whatever it was seeded with
   forever. If turning a real day's work into a bench case is a chore, it will not happen, and the
   axes will be beside the point regardless of how good they are. So: what does it cost, in
   commands, to promote something he actually ran into a bench example?

`--expect` by substring is not wrong; it is a FORMAT check being read as a CORRECTNESS check. Say
which it is before adding to it.

issues.title: Where does a NODE-scoped automation live? .project/automations.json is project-scoped by name
issues.body:
Where does a NODE-scoped automation live? .project/automations.json is project-scoped and the governed writer says so in its name. Two of the three known customers -- restarting this node, verifying this node's catalog -- are node concerns. The sovereign dir is the obvious home, beside config.json, node.json and model-rates.v1.json.

ANSWERED 2026-08-12, as the item itself proposed: the sovereign dir, beside config.json, node.json
and model-rates.v1.json.

    <declaredBase>/.refarm/automations.json     the NODE's
    <project>/.project/automations.json          the project's, found by walking UP from cwd

Both scopes exist and neither is a degenerate case of the other (spec D8). A nightly job about a
vault is the vault's; a restart is the node's, and the node has no repository to be found from.

THE EXECUTOR DOES NOT FORK. `runDueScheduledWork` merges the two adapters and runs one pass -- two
runs would mean two reports, two ledger passes, and a caller stitching them back together, which
is three places for the halves to disagree about what fired. An id in both scopes resolves to the
node's, stated rather than left to be discovered.

ONE IMPLEMENTATION, NOT TWO. The node adapter is the project adapter with `documentPath` supplied;
every line of validation, normalisation and scheduling is shared. A second implementation would
have been a second place for the trigger vocabulary to drift, and the two would have agreed right
up until one was edited.

THE NODE ADAPTER DOES NOT WALK UP, and there is a test that says so: a node standing inside a
repository must not silently adopt that repository's automations as its own.

THE FIRE-ONCE LEDGER MOVED TOO, and it was the same bug one layer down: it lived under `cwd`, so a
node automation ticked from two directories would consult two ledgers and fire twice -- precisely
the duplication the ledger exists to prevent. It is the node's now, with an explicit `base` option
so a test that wants everything inside one temp tree says which node it is rather than inferring
one from the working directory.

issues.title: Which cron parser? None exists, the repo is dependency-light, and cron is subtly easy to get wrong
issues.body:
Which cron parser? None exists, this repo is deliberately dependency-light, and cron is subtly easy to get wrong (day-of-week versus day-of-month). Vendoring something tested likely beats hand-rolling, and the choice deserves the same source-and-date discipline every other external dependency here now carries.

ANSWERED BY RE-MEASUREMENT 2026-08-11, not by a decision. "None exists" was false: the parser is in
packages/windmill/src/local-scheduler.js, hand-rolled and zero-dependency.

AND IT ALREADY GETS THE TRAP THIS ITEM WAS FILED ABOUT. Day-of-month versus day-of-week: when BOTH
fields are restricted, cron matches EITHER, not both. The implementation reads
`domDue || dowDue`, with the two single-restriction cases separated above it. Correct, and now
pinned by a test that says so in words rather than leaving the next reader to re-derive it.

SO NO DEPENDENCY IS NEEDED, and the reason is stronger than "we already wrote one". Every cron
library answers "when is the next occurrence" or throws. This repository needs THREE STATES --
due / not due / undecidable (spec D4) -- and a thrown exception swallowed by a catch is precisely
how "undecidable" becomes "not due", which is the daily-handoff failure that opened ISS-066. A
vendored parser would still need our own three-state layer on top of it, so the dependency would
buy parsing we already have and none of the part that matters.

WHAT THE PARSER DOES NOT DO, recorded so nobody assumes otherwise: no `@yearly`/`@monthly`/
`@reboot`, no step-on-range (`1-9/2`), no month or weekday NAMES (JAN, MON), no `L`/`W`/`#`. Each
of those returns `unsupported` rather than a wrong answer, which is the safe direction. Add one
when an automation needs it.
issues.resolved_by: re-measurement 2026-08-11: a parser already exists in packages/windmill and gets the trap right

issues.title: rcdc5 automation is blocked on P1: a pending prompt's lifetime is its asker's, and nothing resumes an effort
issues.body:
rcdc5 as a workspace-scoped automation consumer is BLOCKED on two named pieces, and the blocker is a declared principle rather than an oversight: pending_prompt.rs states P1, `a pending prompt's lifetime is its asker's lifetime, nothing persists`, and nothing resumes a persisted non-terminal effort. Until both change, an automation that waits for an MFA push cannot survive a restart, and 'waiting for a human' is indistinguishable from 'dead'.

HALF CLOSED 2026-08-11, and the half that closed is the sentence this item is named for:
"waiting for a human" is now distinguishable from "dead".

WHAT WAS MEASURED FIRST, and it reframed the work: the trail has ALWAYS remembered decisions
durably -- `OperationRecord` in a JSON file, matched by `standingDecision`, which is what stops a
wizard re-asking something already settled. What nothing remembered was a question STILL WAITING.
So a background run that asked and died left no trace of having asked, and its next run asked
again. That is the operator's own complaint about the VPN, one layer above the prompt hub.

    decision made      -> durable
    question waiting   -> died with the asker

SHIPPED, in @refarm.dev/operation-consent-v1:

  OperationQuestion             asked, not yet decided -- requestId, purpose, requester, expiresAt
  standingQuestion()            PURE: outstanding | expired | none
  OperationTrail.readQuestions? OPTIONAL, so a trail that cannot remember says so by absence
  runOperationConsent           records BEFORE asking, closes in a `finally`, and returns a new
                                `already-asked` outcome instead of publishing a second card

P1 IS NOT WEAKENED and was not touched. `pending_prompt.rs` keeps its principle exactly -- a
PROMPT's lifetime is its asker's, nothing persists, no garbage collection, no stale-answer
problem. This is a different record in a different place: the prompt still dies with its asker;
the memory that it was asked does not. That is the "second kind of prompt" the automation spec's
D9 named as the alternative to revisiting P1, and it turned out to belong in the consent trail
rather than in the hub.

EXPIRY IS BY TIME, NEVER BY SWEEPING. A run killed outright cannot close its own record, so the
record carries the asker's deadline (24h default) and reads as `expired` past it -- which falls
through and asks again ON PURPOSE. A record that blocked the question forever would turn one
`kill -9` into permanent silence about that operation.

STILL OPEN, and it is the other half this item names:

1. THE ANSWER IS STILL EPHEMERAL. `runOperationConsent` writes the decision record in the ASKING
   process, so an operator answering after that process is gone has nobody to write it down. The
   durable question means the next run knows not to ask twice; it does not yet mean the answer
   survives. Closing that needs the node to record the decision itself -- Rust, and a real design
   decision about who owns the write.

2. NOTHING RESUMES A PERSISTED NON-TERMINAL EFFORT. Untouched. `load_persisted_efforts` restores
   the state at boot and nothing picks it up.

THE OTHER HALF CLOSED 2026-08-12. A question whose asker is gone can now be answered, and the
answer TAKES EFFECT.

WHAT THE FIRST DESIGN GOT WRONG, found by asking what a recorded decision actually does: a
decision and its application happen TOGETHER in operation-consent-v1, and `already-decided`
deliberately does not re-apply. So recording an answer out of band would have produced a decision
that never took effect -- worse than being unable to decide, because it looks like it worked.

The fix is that the standing question carries the WHOLE REQUEST, not just what a surface needs to
display it. A request holds its own `changes`, with a complete before/after per file, which is
exactly what applying it later needs.

    refarm resume --answer <id> --authorize|--decline

--authorize and --decline are both required to be explicit. A missing flag is not "probably yes"
and not "probably no"; it is a malformed instruction, and the answer is the one thing a consent
surface must never guess.

AND IT IMPLEMENTS ISS-118's SECOND CHECK. Before applying, every change's `before` is compared
against the file as it is NOW. Any drift refuses with `stale` and names the files: the gap between
asking and answering is exactly where a card sits on a phone for an hour, and the operator
authorised a change to the file they were SHOWN, not to this one. A refused answer leaves the
question standing, because nothing was decided.

Five states, and only two of them are ordinary: applied, declined, expired, unanswerable (a record
written before requests were stored -- reported honestly rather than offered a button that fails),
and stale.

STILL OPEN, and it is now a smaller thing than this item started as: nothing resumes a persisted
non-terminal effort. `load_persisted_efforts` restores the state at boot and nothing picks it up.
That is a different mechanism from consent and does not block the VPN case any more.

issues.title: The openai-codex token expires and nothing in this repo refreshes it on either node
issues.body:
This item is the "the openai-codex token expires and nothing in this repo auto-refreshes it on EITHER node" clause of the paragraph below, which is reproduced whole so the reason for the non-isolation travels with it.

WHAT IS NOT ISOLATED, named rather than left to be discovered: SILO_HOME isolates the STORE, not the credential -- inherited by copy on purpose, since isolation that forced re-auth would not get used; the openai-codex token expires and nothing in this repo auto-refreshes it on EITHER node; there is no `stop` subcommand, and --reset has a documented, unclosed TOCTOU race with `start`.

OPERATOR RULING 2026-08-12: the alignment is agreed -- the node SAYS the credential is expired
rather than silently renewing it -- and he names an opportunity on top of it.

His words: make it easy to develop renewals that can be done REMOTELY. Decouple what genuinely
requires him running commands ON THE NODE to prepare, from what could naturally happen over termux,
Telegram, a PWA or whatever surface he happens to be holding.

That is the same axis this session already built the primitives for, and it is worth naming so the
work is not repeated:

    createAttendedOperatorChannel   a question reaches the devices with NO terminal in the race
    OperationQuestion + resume      the node remembers it asked, and says so, across restarts
    resume --answer <id>            the answer lands and TAKES EFFECT after the asker is gone

So a renewal is not a new mechanism. It is: detect expiry -> put a durable question -> the operator
answers from whatever surface he is on -> the node applies it. What is missing is the FIRST step
(nothing detects and reports expiry as its own state) and the boundary he asks for: which parts of
a renewal genuinely need a local command, and which are just a question with an answer.

DESIGN NOTE FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT: separate the two before writing either. A renewal flow that
assumes a terminal will be rewritten the first time it is needed from a phone, and a flow that
assumes a phone will fail on the step that genuinely needs the node's own filesystem.

THE FIRST STEP IS DONE 2026-08-12, and measuring it found the item happening LIVE.

`~/.silo/identity.json` records `tokens.oauthCredentials["openai-codex"].expires`. On the operator's
node that timestamp was 2026-08-07 19:29 -- the token had been EXPIRED FOR FIVE DAYS and nothing in
this repository said so. `model doctor` probed whether the endpoint answers, which is a different
question: an expired credential and an unreachable host are two facts with two remedies, and a
doctor reporting only the second sends an operator to debug a network.

    credentialLifetime()      PURE, injected clock: valid | expired | unknown
    ModelDoctorStatus.credential   reported beside the probe, never folded into it
    the human line            printed BEFORE the probe's early returns, so the case where it
                              matters most -- a skipped or failed probe -- is not the one where
                              it never gets said

THREE STATES, and `unknown` earns its place twice: a provider with no OAuth entry (a keyless local
model has no credential to be valid) and an OAuth entry carrying no `expires`. Neither is "probably
fine", and rendering either as valid is an absence dressed as a reassurance.

THE HUMAN LINE PRINTS NOTHING FOR `unknown`, on purpose. A doctor that announces
"credential: unknown" for every keyless provider teaches an operator to skim the line, and the day
it says EXPIRED they skim that too. It warns at three days and states the fact at zero.

STILL OPEN, and it is the operator's own framing: WHICH PARTS OF A RENEWAL GENUINELY NEED THE NODE.
A `refresh` token is present beside the expired `access` one, so a renewal is possible without a
browser -- but whether that exchange belongs to the node acting alone, or to a durable question
answered from a phone, is the boundary he asked to have drawn before either is written.

issues.title: refarm check reports ok:true while refarm health reports config_node_drift on the same node
issues.body:
FOUND 2026-08-09 while running the after-edit gate for the ledger migration, and it is the
catalogued shape again: an instrument reporting a result it has not earned.

MEASURED, in this order:

  1. `refarm agent finish --lane after-edit --run --json` FAILED with failedStepId "check",
     recommendation config_node_drift: "The replicated config graph node differs from the local
     .refarm/config.json."
  2. `git stash push -u` (my four changed files away, tree clean) then
     `refarm check --next-action --json` -> ok: true, recommendations: [].
  3. Tree dirtied with an UNRELATED file (a newline appended to README.md) ->
     `refarm check --next-action --json` -> ok: true, recommendations: [].
  4. Same clean tree, `refarm health --json` -> config_node_drift IS present:
     "graph node revision sha256:334404f2... differs from local sha256:6d..." (twice), alongside
     stale_build findings.

So the divergence exists on this node REGARDLESS of the working tree. What changes with the working
tree is whether the mandated entry point LOOKS: `refarm check --next-action --json` runs the
"affected" profile (selection.profile: "affected", validationScope: "dirtyTree"), and a change under
.project/** pulls the config-node auditor in while a change under docs/ or README.md does not. The
result is that a real, standing node defect reports ok: true from the command CLAUDE.md tells every
agent to trust, and only becomes visible if the slice happens to touch the right path.

Two states where three are needed, one more time: "audited and clean" and "not audited" produce the
identical ok: true. The third state -- "this auditor did not run for this change set" -- is not
reported anywhere in the envelope. Note the auditor itself already got this right one layer down: it
distinguishes config_node_unreachable ("could not check") from a clean pass, precisely so a failed
read cannot read as fine (packages/health/src/auditors/config-node.js:150-168). The selection layer
above it then re-introduces the collapse it was written to avoid.

THE NODE CONDITION UNDERNEATH, recorded so it is not lost with this item: the graph's RefarmConfig
node and ~/.refarm/config.json disagree, which is the expected consequence of the 2026-08-08 node
update (ISS-067 -- connections.ovpn-serpro, trusted_plugins and approvedPermissions were written to
the operator's real config) with nothing re-syncing the graph node afterwards. The remedy the
recommendation names is "Re-run the runtime to re-sync the RefarmConfig node" -- a restart, which is
the operator's call because it interrupts whatever the node is serving, exactly as the handoff
already says of the other restart-shaped findings. It was deliberately NOT done by the slice that
found it.

WHAT A FIX LOOKS LIKE (not taken here): either the check envelope reports which auditors were skipped
for this change set, or the config-node audit is unconditional because node-state findings are not a
function of which files a slice edited. The second is the smaller change and the honest one -- a
node's config drifting has nothing to do with the diff.

CORRECTED 2026-08-09 (fix round 1) — THE PRECEDENCE CLAIM ABOVE WAS WRONG, AND THE EXPERIMENT COULD
NOT HAVE PROVEN IT. The paragraphs above read the stash experiment as showing the drift "exists on
this node REGARDLESS of the working tree" and therefore predates this slice. `git stash` moves files
inside the REPOSITORY; ~/.refarm/config.json is outside it and was never touched by any of those
four commands, so the experiment could not distinguish "pre-existing" from "caused by an edit made
outside the repository". It was the second: the controller edited ~/.refarm/config.json before Task 4
to declare this workspace's ledger, and nothing re-synced the RefarmConfig graph node afterwards.
Step 4 (health on a clean tree) shows only that the drift is not a function of the working tree —
which is true, and is a weaker statement than the one it was used for.

WHAT SURVIVES THE CORRECTION, unchanged and still the reason this item is open: steps 1-4 measured a
real REPORTING asymmetry. `refarm check --next-action --json` returned ok: true on the same node, at
the same moment, at which `refarm health --json` reported config_node_drift — because check's
affected profile pulls the config-node auditor in only when the change set touches .project/**. The
cause of the drift is irrelevant to that; a node-state finding is not a function of which files a

RESOLVED PART: the operator restarted the runtime on 2026-08-09. The graph node re-synced, the drift
is gone, `refarm check --next-action --json` returns ok: true, and both agent lanes pass. The restart
itself surfaced ISS-084 — `refarm runtime restart --json` reported ok: false with a null error for a

issues.title: runtime restart --json reports ok:false with a null error after a restart that succeeded
issues.body:
REPORTED BY THE OPERATOR 2026-08-09, while clearing the config drift that ISS-083 describes.
`refarm runtime restart --json` returned, verbatim:

  {"ok": false, "error": null, "message": null, "nextAction": "refarm runtime ensure --wait --next-command"}

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED: the restart SUCCEEDED. Following the handoff confirmed the runtime ready and
the RefarmConfig drift gone; `refarm check --next-action --json` returned ok: true afterwards. So the
command reported failure for an act it had just performed, with a null error and a null message —
unreadable to an operator and unreadable to an agent, which under CLAUDE.md's JSON handoff rules is
told to inspect `ok` and follow `nextCommands` before deciding anything.

THE MECHANISM, read from the code rather than guessed:

  - apps/refarm/src/commands/runtime.ts:235-238 — after spawning, `ready` is probed ONLY when
    --wait is passed: `const ready = opts.wait ? await waitForRuntimeReady() : undefined`.
  - :244-248 — the JSON payload is then built from `{...payload}` with `ready` spread in only when
    it is not undefined. Without --wait, `payload` is the snapshot taken by
    `resolveRuntimeStartCommand` BEFORE the restart — i.e. describing a runtime that had just been
    stopped one statement earlier.
  - apps/refarm/src/commands/runtime-status.ts:181-190 — `runtimeOperationOk` judges a restart with
    `runtimeIsHealthy(payload)` (`activeEngine !== "unknown" && !issue && ready !== false`). Against
    a pre-restart snapshot that verdict is about a state that no longer exists by the time it prints.
  - :263 — `if (opts.wait && !ready) process.exitCode = 1`. So without --wait the envelope says
    `ok: false` while the process exits 0: the two channels disagree about the same run.

WHY `error` AND `message` ARE NULL: this envelope carries the runtime's state under `issue`, not
under `error`/`message`, so those keys are emitted as null for every restart. A consumer reading
`ok: false` finds nothing that says WHAT failed, because nothing did.

THE SHAPE: two states where three are needed, again. "The restart failed" and "nobody looked after
the restart" produce the identical `ok: false`. `status` already got this right one function up —
runtime-status.ts:167-179 documents at length why a report is always `ok: true` and why acts are
judged by health — but an act whose result was never observed is a third state that reasoning does
not cover: not healthy, not unhealthy, UNOBSERVED.

WHAT A FIX LOOKS LIKE (not taken here): either re-probe readiness before judging a restart even
without --wait, or report `ok` for the ACT (the stop and the spawn both succeeded) and leave
readiness to `ready`/`issue` where a caller can see it — with `ready: null` meaning unobserved
rather than false. The second matches this repo's own precedent that an unobserved value is not a
negative one. Whichever is chosen, `ok: false` with a null error and a null message must not survive.

latest on the 8.5 line. `^8.5.23` keeps the same major, matching the nanoid entry's reasoning.

WHY BOUNDARY STYLE AND NOT JUST A BUMP, which is what this item asked to decide: a `<=X: ^Y` pin
whose X is not the CURRENT advisory boundary reads as protection and is not. Bumping X alone
fixes today; stating the boundary the advisory states makes the NEXT drift readable without

issues.title: The decompress advisory is accepted on the grounds that it has no patch, and a patch now exists
issues.body:
RE-MEASURED 2026-08-11, and THIS ITEM WAS WRONG — in the same way as the comment it was
correcting, and for the same reason.

The item says: "pnpm audit reports decompress <=4.2.1 -> patched >=4.2.2 ... The no-patch half of
the recorded justification is now FALSE."

  npm view decompress versions   ->  41 versions, ending at 4.2.1
  npm view decompress dist-tags  ->  latest: 4.2.1
  override to ^4.2.2             ->  ERR_PNPM_NO_MATCHING_VERSION

THERE IS NO 4.2.2. The `patched >=4.2.2` in `pnpm audit` is ADVISORY METADATA — a statement about
which version WOULD carry the fix — not a claim that it exists. The original justification's
central sentence was true, and this item disputed it by reading the same metadata the comment's
author had read. Neither asked the registry. That is the lesson worth keeping, and it is now
written into the exception itself.

WHAT WAS TRUE, and is corrected on the record:

  1. THE SEVERITY IS CRITICAL, not moderate. That is why `pnpm audit --audit-level=high` exits 0
     while its own metadata reports `critical: 1` — the count includes what ignoreGhsas
     suppresses, the gate does not.

  2. THE SUPPRESSION DOES NOT SUPPRESS. GHSA-h39j-r5qq-r9mm reports the SAME package, range and
     (absent) patch, and is not on the list, so decompress fails the moderate-prod gate anyway.
     The ignore hid the severity and bought nothing. It is deliberately NOT extended to the
     sibling: silencing a real finding with no available fix is a different act from accepting
     one.

  3. THE DEV-ONLY REACH IS NOW VERIFIED, which this item correctly noted had never been
     re-checked. `pnpm why decompress -r` resolves exactly one path:
     decompress@4.2.1 <- @bytecodealliance/weval <- componentize-js <- @bytecodealliance/jco —
     the build-time WASM toolchain. It does not reach a shipped artifact.

THE EXCEPTION STANDS, with its justification rewritten to say all of the above and to name the
trigger: a published decompress >4.2.1, or jco dropping weval. Re-check the REGISTRY, not the
advisory page.

issues.title: CI audits at three different scopes and the moderate-prod one is red
issues.body:
RESOLVED 2026-08-11 by the operator's ruling: **`pnpm audit --audit-level=moderate --prod` is the
gate, with a re-check date on every accepted advisory.** Option (c) of the three this item listed.

WHAT WAS TRUE AND IS NOW ANSWERED: four audit invocations ran at three scopes and nothing said
which one had to hold. `--audit-level=high` passed while `moderate --prod` failed, so "the audit
is green" named no particular fact. `before-push`'s security step was the `high` one; it is the
moderate gate now.

WHY THE DATE IS THE WHOLE POINT, and not a refinement: four advisories fail this scope and none
has a reachable fix, so a bare `moderate --prod` is red on arrival — and a gate red on arrival is
one an operator learns to bypass. The two mechanisms that solved that before both accepted things
FOREVER, and both went stale with their justifications still sitting there looking current:
the postcss pin (ISS-086) and a CRITICAL `ignoreGhsas` entry whose own comment admitted it had
not been re-verified (ISS-087).

SHIPPED:
  scripts/security/accepted-advisories.mjs  the five acceptances, each with WHY, a TRIGGER, and
                                            a recheckBy date
  scripts/security/audit-gate.mjs           the gate
  pnpm run security:gate                    also wired into `refarm agent finish --lane before-push`

FOUR WAYS TO FAIL, and only the first is what a security gate normally has. All four proven by
poisoning a live run:
  UNACCEPTED  reported and undeclared                     (removed an entry -> named it)
  EXPIRED     accepted, still reported, date passed       (moved a date back -> exit 1, and the
                                                           message prints that entry's TRIGGER,
                                                           so it says what to re-check)
  STALE       accepted and no longer reported             (the exception outlived its advisory)
  HIDDEN      severity counts do not reconcile

HIDDEN is this item's sharpest observation made mechanical. `pnpm audit` COUNTS an ignoreGhsas
advisory in `metadata.vulnerabilities` and OMITS it from `advisories`, which is why
`--audit-level=high` exits 0 while printing `critical: 1` in the same JSON. The gate adds the
declared `suppressed` entries back and fails on any surplus — so the suppression is no longer
invisible, and a silenced advisory nobody wrote down is as loud as a brand-new one.

CURRENT STATE: 4 reported, 5 declared (4 reported + 1 suppressed critical), next re-check
2026-10-10. Gate green.

  turbo run build 139/139 · turbo run test 282/282 · before-push green end to end

issues.title: The operator requirements R1-R12 exist only in Markdown and are invisible to every instrument

Eleven are Parcial and one (R12, the executive view) is Ausente. NONE of them exists in .project/requirements.json. issues.title: refarm task list --json writes to the node on every read
issues.body: MEASURED 2026-08-10 while closing the footguns before the directory-independence burn-down. A sweep of 72 read-only invocations (the 36 probeable commands, run twice each from the repository) changed exactly one file on the operator's real node: ~/.refarm/sessions/task-session.v1.json. Bisected to a single command: `refarm task list --json` rewrites it on every read, updating `updatedAt` and stamping `lastCommand: "list"` (size unchanged 9648 -> 9648; only mtime and those fields move). WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: (1) it makes a read command a writer, so the node's task-session record cannot distinguish 'this effort was touched' from 'somebody listed'; `lastCommand` and `updatedAt` are written by an observer, which is the same shape as a report that claims more than it measured. (2) It is a live hazard for scripts/directory-independence.mjs, which runs every probed command once per directory plus a control run -- a mutating entry would write to the operator's real node three times per probe invocation, forever, and the probe is meant to be run often. THE READ-ONLY RULE HAD NO OBSERVATION BEHIND IT: `task list` is called list, it prints, it exits 0, and it looks read-only from every angle a reviewer has. That is why the probe now snapshots the sovereign dir around a full run and WARNS naming the files that changed (warn, not block: the daemon shares that directory and may write concurrently, and a check that fires on the environment trains its reader to ignore it). UNTIL THIS IS FIXED, `task list` is excluded from PROBE_COMMANDS with this id as the reason -- so 1 of the 36 probeable invocations is deliberately unmeasured, named rather than silently dropped. FIX SHAPE: the read path should not persist; if a read genuinely needs to refresh a cache, that write belongs behind an explicit flag or a separate verb, not inside `list`.

issues.title: refarm resume --json returns ok:true with an EMPTY project block outside the repository
issues.body:
CONVICTED by scripts/directory-independence.mjs on 2026-08-10. Verdict: differs-undeclared, scope node. Sixteen diverging field paths: project.blockers, project.context, project.currentPhase, project.currentTasks, project.nextActions, project.openQuestions, project.path, project.timestamp, and all eight project.truncation.{blockers,currentTasks,nextActions,openQuestions}.{returned,total}. Directories: /home/s095407044/github/refarm vs /tmp vs ~/git/rcdc5. environmentPressure.signals was EXCLUDED as time-variant by the control pair, so all sixteen are real.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY RETURNS from /tmp, measured: ok:true, project.path null, currentPhase null, context empty string, 0 currentTasks, 0 nextActions, 0 blockers, truncation null.

THIS IS THE ZERO THAT IS NOT A ZERO, at the front door. CLAUDE.md section 4 mandates 'refarm resume --json' at the start of EVERY slice and tells the agent to trust its nextCommands. From outside the repository it reports no work, no blockers and no next actions with ok:true, and nothing in the envelope distinguishes 'this node has no pending work' from 'I did not read any project'. Worse: the truncation field is null -- the field the 2026-08-08 slice added SPECIFICALLY so a partial read could not masquerade as a complete one now reads as 'nothing was truncated' rather than 'nothing was read'. That slice fixed the instrument lying about 5-of-24; this is the same instrument lying about 0-of-24 one directory over.

SCOPE DECISION, AND WHY IT IS A CONVICTION RATHER THAN A DECLARATION: resume is MIXED. Runtime, model, session and ledger are node facts -- the ledger block is correctly identical from all three directories, which proves the node path works -- while the project block is genuinely this directory's project. Declaring project.* as allowed-varying would make the row pass and leave the empty-block-with-ok-true untouched, which is declaring the defect instead of closing it.

FIX SHAPE, to be decided in the burn-down after auditing the call sites: the project block needs three states, not two -- a project was read (contents), there is no project here (explicitly absent, never an empty list), and the project could not be read (a named failure). apps/refarm/src/commands/resume.ts carries 3 bare process.cwd() sites, and packages/cli/src/project-handoff.ts:100 resolves .project/handoff.json as a RELATIVE path -- the same positional resolution the ledger slice named when it refused to mirror 'refarm project' for the issues command.

issues.title: doctor reports host.packageManager as pnpm here and npm from anywhere else
issues.body:
CONVICTED by scripts/directory-independence.mjs on 2026-08-10. Verdict: differs-undeclared, scope node. Diverging field paths: host.packageManager, nextAction, nextActions, nextCommand, nextCommands, recommendations, warnings, warningCount.

MEASURED VALUES: host.packageManager is 'pnpm' from /home/s095407044/github/refarm and 'npm' from BOTH /tmp and ~/git/rcdc5.

THE FIELD NAME IS THE ARGUMENT: a field called host.* cannot depend on which directory the operator is standing in. Either the value is the project's package manager and the name is a lie, or the resolution is wrong. Both are defects and they are not the same defect.

The seven other diverging fields are DOWNSTREAM: nextAction, nextCommands, recommendations, warnings and warningCount are derived from the wrong packageManager, so the doctor's ADVICE changes with the caller's directory too. That is the part that costs -- 'refarm doctor' is what an operator or agent runs to be told what to do next, and it currently says something different depending on where you were standing when you asked.

THE RATCHET'S LARGEST CLUSTER IS BEHIND THIS: packages/config/src/package-manager.js carries TEN bare process.cwd() sites, the single biggest file in the 103-site count, and apps/refarm/src/commands/doctor.ts carries three more. This is the first time that cluster has been tied to a WRONG ANSWER rather than to a shape count, which is the entire reason this slice measures by consequence.

DO NOT CONFLATE THE COMPANION: 'refarm package-manager --json' is declared scope PROJECT in the probe and legitimately varies (pnpm here, npm elsewhere) -- detecting THIS tree's package manager is its job. The defect is doctor consuming that project fact and reporting it under a host.* name.

issues.title: plugin list reports the node's own plugin as unresolved from any other directory
issues.body:
CONVICTED by scripts/directory-independence.mjs on 2026-08-10. Verdict: differs-undeclared, scope node. Diverging field path: plugins.

MEASURED: from /home/s095407044/github/refarm the single installed plugin reports packageSource 'workspace' with packageDir '/home/s095407044/github/refarm/packages/agent'; from /tmp the SAME plugin reports packageSource 'unresolved' with packageDir null. Same id (@refarm/agent), same version (0.1.0), same source (bundled) -- only the provenance fields collapse.

WHY IT MATTERS: a plugin is installed into the NODE's sovereign dir, and 'plugin status' (which reports what the daemon has LOADED) is correctly identical from all three directories. So the node knows perfectly well where its plugin came from; 'plugin list' re-derives that provenance from the caller's working tree instead of reading it. 'unresolved' is not a neutral word here -- it is what an operator sees before deciding whether a plugin is trustworthy, and it appears for a plugin that is fully resolved on the node.

This is the same family as the VPN defect the 2026-08-07 slice closed: node state presented through a working-tree lens, correct exactly where it is developed and wrong everywhere the operator actually stands. apps/refarm/src/commands/plugin-shared.ts carries 2 bare process.cwd() sites; audit before substituting, because resolving a WORKSPACE package legitimately needs a workspace root.

issues.title: surface list reads the caller's directory .refarm/config.json instead of the node's
issues.body:
CONVICTED by scripts/directory-independence.mjs on 2026-08-10. Verdict: differs-undeclared, scope node. Diverging field paths: configPath, root, surfaces.

MEASURED: from the repository, root '/home/s095407044/github/refarm', configPath '/home/s095407044/github/refarm/.refarm/config.json', 3 surfaces. From /tmp, root '/tmp', configPath '/tmp/.refarm/config.json', 0 surfaces.

THIS IS THE FIXTURE DEFECT, EXACTLY AS THE 2026-08-07 SLICE NAMED IT. That slice found ovpn-serpro visible only from this checkout and recorded the finding in these words: 'visible from the repo, invisible everywhere else was never the feature working -- it was the SYMPTOM, the CLI reading a fixture and presenting it as the node's catalog.' The repo's .refarm/config.json is a gitignored dev fixture written while building that very feature. surface list is still reading it and presenting its three surfaces as the node's.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR DAILY USE: surfaces are how the operator reaches this node from Termux, the PWA and Telegram. A surface catalog that empties when he runs the command from anywhere but one checkout is the difference between 'my node offers three ways in' and 'my node offers none', decided by his shell's working directory. The honest empty answer -- 0 surfaces from every directory -- would at least be legible; 3-here and 0-there is the state that reads as working.

apps/refarm/src/commands/surface.ts carries 3 bare process.cwd() sites. The fix is the same one connection.ts took in d8f850b8: resolve declaredBase() rather than the caller's directory.

issues.title: Twenty-one read-only commands are probeable and not yet probed, held under a ratchet
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-10 while building the coverage test. The CLI has 187 leaf commands, not the 64 top-level ones the first count reported, and 181 of them accept --json -- the flag is nearly universal here. Of those, 64 require a positional argument the probe has no fixture for and are excluded by a DERIVED rule, 35 are probed, and 85 needed a decision.

Of the 85, twenty-one are read-only candidates that SHOULD be probed and have not been given a scope and a written reason yet: agent doctor, auth list, config plugins list, hardening, health audit, health policy, health suggest-policy, issues validate, model doctor, model env, process status, project automations list, project automations validate, provision list, records analyze, release check, release plan, workspace execution, workspace mounts, workspace sources declarations, workspace status.

They are NOT in the probe yet for one reason, and it is the ISS-091 lesson: `refarm task list` looked read-only from every angle a reviewer has -- it is called list, it prints, it exits 0 -- and it rewrites the node's task-session file on every read. Admitting twenty-one commands to an instrument that runs each of them four times per invocation, on the strength of their names, would repeat that mistake twenty-one times. Each needs the same treatment the 35 got: verify it writes nothing, decide node or project, write the reason.

THE BACKLOG IS RATCHETED, NOT MERELY LISTED. scripts/directory-independence-exclusions.mjs exports NOT_YET_PROBED_CEILING = 21 and apps/refarm/test/commands/probe-coverage.test.ts fails if the count exceeds it -- same discipline as no-os-resolution.mjs's BASELINE_MAX_OFFENDING_SITES. A new command may be excluded as mutating, interactive or expensive; it may not join this backlog. Lower the ceiling in the same commit that graduates a command into PROBE_COMMANDS.

Probing all 21 would raise the measured surface from 35 to 56 of the 116 commands that are probeable in principle (181 with --json, minus 64 needing arguments, minus the mutating and interactive ones).

issues.title: The directory-independence probe has no CI home until a seeded node fixture exists
issues.body:
DECISION 2026-08-10, taken from measurement rather than from the plan, which had said CI would run a subset of the probe and report its coverage as a fraction.

MEASURED under an empty REFARM_HOME, which is what CI has: `workspace list` returns [] from every directory and scores `same`; `connection status` does the same. `plugin list` and `surface list` still differ, because they read the WORKING TREE rather than the node's catalog.

So a CI run would catch two of the four real convictions and report agreement between two ABSENCES as `same` for the rest.
