issues.title: A conformance test's sentinel is the operator's configured model route
issues.body:
FOUND 2026-08-12, in `refarm model doctor`'s own output on the operator's node.

    current: openai-codex/__refarm_ancestor_option_probe__
    probe:   __refarm_ancestor_option_probe__

That sentinel exists in exactly ONE place in this repository:
`apps/refarm/test/architecture/ancestor-option-conformance.test.ts`. A TEST wrote its probe value
into the operator's real model route, and every `model current` since has reported it as his
configured model.

WHERE, and it is not where ISS-109 looked: `~/.silo/identity.json`, in three fields --
`tokens.modelId`, `tokens.modelFallbackModelId`, `tokens.modelBaseUrl`. ISS-109 was written about
`~/.refarm/config.json`. The silo is a SECOND store nobody thought to check, and both are reached
through HOME -- which is why redirecting HOME, rather than blocklisting known paths, was the right
shape for the containment.

THE HOLE IS ALREADY CLOSED. The file's mtime is 2026-08-11 01:31, hours before the home containment
shipped. Verified today from inside a real `apps/refarm` test: a write to a LITERAL path under the
operator's home throws.

MEASUREMENT NOTE, because the first attempt to verify this got it backwards: probing with
`os.homedir()` SUCCEEDS under containment, because containment REDIRECTS HOME rather than
blocklisting it, so `os.homedir()` already points at the disposable tree. Reading that success as
an escape is the trap; only a literal path distinguishes containment from redirection. The
permanent test asserts both halves and says so.

WHAT REMAINS IS OPERATOR DATA, and it is his call rather than mine: his model route still holds the
sentinel. `refarm model reset` restores the built-in default for the provider
(`openai-codex` -> `gpt-5.5`), and `--scope worker` / `--scope monitor` do the same per scope. What
the route held BEFORE the test overwrote it is not recoverable from anything in this repository --
choosing a value would be inventing his configuration, which is the same class of act as the one
that caused this.
RE-MEASURED 2026-08-18, AND THE BLAST RADIUS IS WIDER THAN THE ROUTE. Two BudgetObservation records on the operator's live node carry `gen_ai.request.model: __refarm_ancestor_option_probe__`, spawner `capability-dispatch`. So the conformance test did not merely poison a config field that a later read could correct — it caused DISPATCHES that were recorded, permanently, in the node's spend ledger. Those two rows are now part of the denominator every quota report reads (ISS-073).

The route half is repairable by writing the right value back. The record half is not: a budget observation is an append-only fact about something that happened, and "it did not really happen, a test did it" is not a state the record can express. The honest options are to leave them and know what they are, or to give the record a way to say a row was synthetic — and the second is a contract change, not a cleanup.

WHAT MAKES THIS RECUR: the test drives the real CLI against the real node base. Nothing about it is sandboxed to a scratch SOVEREIGN_BASE, so every field the CLI would touch in production it touches here. That is the fix worth making — one env var in the harness — and it closes the class rather than this instance.

issues.title: A second account of one provider destroys the first: the silo keys credentials by provider alone
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-12, against a real SiloCore with SILO_HOME redirected — not read from the code:

    1) after personal login : {"github-copilot":{"account":"pessoal","token":"gho_PESSOAL",...}}
    2) after corporate login: {"github-copilot":{"account":"corporativa","token":"gho_CORP",...}}
    personal credential still present? false

`tokens.oauthCredentials` is keyed by PROVIDER and holds ONE slot. `sow` spreads the existing map
and writes `[credential.provider]`, so authenticating a second account of the same provider
silently overwrites the first. No error, no warning, no copy kept. This is the same class of
accident as ISS-121 — an irreversible write to the operator's source of truth that nothing
reports — with the difference that here it is the DESIGN doing it, not a stray test.

WHY IT BLOCKS STATED WORK. The operator has three quotas across two providers: GitHub Copilot
personal, GitHub Copilot corporate, and Codex personal. Two of the three are the same provider.
Under today's shape they cannot coexist, and the act of adding the second destroys the first.

NOTE THE INTERACTION WITH TODAY'S sow FIX. Making an expired credential re-prompt (commit
aaf1a8b2) is correct and makes this MORE reachable: the wizard now re-authenticates on expiry,
which is exactly the moment a second account would be entered.

PRIOR ART, already proven next door rather than to be invented: `agents-lab`'s pi-stack models
identity as `buildProviderAccountKey(provider, account)` throughout its quota-visibility
extensions — `packages/pi-stack/extensions/quota-visibility-billing.ts` extracts Copilot billing
rows keyed by provider AND account, with weekly/monthly caps and share semantics. That is the
same key this repository is missing, and it is also what R4's per-workspace quota split (ISS-064)
and the "which part did refarm not dispatch" question (ISS-073) both need.

THE DECISION IS THE OPERATOR'S, because it is his credential model and it reaches workspaces:
whether an account is a dimension OF the credential key, or credentials are scoped BY workspace
and the workspace carries the account. Both make the destruction impossible; they differ in
where the operator picks which quota a piece of work spends.

WHAT IS SAFE TO DO BEFORE THAT DECISION: refuse to silently replace an existing subscription
credential. A guard needs no new data model and removes the irreversible half of the defect.

issues.title: Nothing can enumerate, export or restore the node's source of truth — a reformat loses it
issues.body:
THE OPERATOR'S OWN FRAMING, 2026-08-12: he needs to be able to bring a node up somewhere else, or on the same machine after a reformat, and says this is why he builds refarm at all.

THE THREE GAPS -- inventory, export, restore -- were shipped and proven by 2026-08-12. What kept this open was that the INSTRUMENT worked and the operator's node was not backed up by it: `backup plan` reported a pile of entries no rule classified.

CLOSED 2026-08-18 (84dd54cf). The pile had already shrunk to ONE by the time it was re-measured -- `hasUndecided` is driven by the `undecidable` list alone, and that list held a single file: `~/.refarm/session.lock`, 57 bytes.

The classification: a lock names a LIVE process, so it is `cache` with a `rebuiltBy`. Carried into a bundle and restored elsewhere it points at a pid that does not exist there, and a stale lock is worse than an absent one -- it can make the restored node refuse to start, or believe a session is already held. Keyed on the `.lock` SUFFIX rather than the filename, because a rule naming `session.lock` would leave the next lock undecidable, which is exactly how this entry came to exist.

MEASURED ON THE REAL NODE AFTERWARDS, which was always the point:
  hasUndecided  true -> false        undecidable 1 -> 0
  bundle        34 files, 1.1MB, `backup verify` ok
  secrets       0 of 3 candidates harvested from the live ~/.silo/identity.json appear anywhere in the bundle
  manifest      names what to re-obtain: telegram.token (re-obtain), ca.key (re-establish), the TLS cert (re-issue)

The silo split holds on his real data, not only in the suite that builds its own node.

THE 104 `foreign` ENTRIES ARE NOT UNDECIDED, and re-measuring settled that: 89 peer ids and 9 databases for namespaces this node does not declare (`complete-http-stream-drip-test`, `repro.db`, `scratch-node-identity-proof.db`), plus the 6 hand-made `config.json.bak-*`. `foreign` IS the decision -- not carried, not deleted, because carrying every undeclared file would bury the ones that stand the node up. The operator's policy of 2026-08-13, already in the layout.

TWO THINGS THIS DOES NOT DECIDE, both the operator's:
1. The bundle needs a DURABLE destination. The one created here lives in scratch; a backup on volatile disk is not a backup.
2. `ca.key` does not travel. Regenerating it is not recovery -- every device that trusted the old one must be re-enrolled by hand -- while `--include-secrets` makes the bundle itself a credential, and a backup is precisely the thing people copy to places they do not think hard about. Recommended: keep the default, and treat the CA key as one deliberate secret rather than turning 34 files into a credential.

issues.title: The requirements-supply hold audit walked three hardcoded names for a four-member profile
issues.body:
FOUND 2026-08-16 while flipping content-projection to consumer-proven, and it is the reason
that flip could not simply be a tag edit.

    scripts/ci/release-boundary-audit.mjs:329   for (const packageName of [ ...3 names... ])
    refarm.config.json  releasePolicy   4 profiles carry the requirements-supply tag

`auditRequirementsSupplyHolds` iterated a hardcoded list of THREE package names while the profile
had FOUR members. `@refarm.dev/content-projection` was in neither that list nor
`CONSUMER_PROVEN_REQUIREMENTS_SUPPLY_PACKAGES`, so the boundary audit had NO OPINION about it.

THE SHARP EDGE: the rule the function exists to enforce -- "must declare candidate-hold until
selected downstream proof" -- never ran against the one package that was actually on hold. The
`candidate-hold` tag was held in place by a single deepEqual in
scripts/ci/test-requirements-supply-handoff.mjs and by nothing else, while release-boundary-audit
reported ok:true about the lane.

SAME CLASS AS ISS-113, one function over in the same file: that item found a `CONSUMER_PULLS` map
here duplicating refarm.config.json and drifting from it. A gate reading its own copy of the thing
it audits is auditing itself.

membership is DERIVED from the requirements-supply tag, so a fifth member is covered the moment it
joins; which members are PROVEN stays an explicit declaration, because deriving that from the same
tags the function audits makes the check a tautology that can never fail. The audit now returns

package the auditor never opened.

issues.title: A doc gate compared a stale document to a hardcoded count, and reported PASS
issues.body:
FOUND 2026-08-16, by watching it NOT fail.

    assert.equal(currentSelection.length, 23);                        // measured
    assert.match(releaseGateDoc, /current\s+22-package\s+selection/); // literal

The first line reads the real selection. The second compares the doc against a hardcoded 22. When

consumer that did not exist) and ISS-124 (a gate reporting ok about packages it never opened).
Here the defect is narrower and meaner: the gate was not blind, it was comparing the doc to a
number it had already measured correctly two lines above and then ignored.

issues.title: A third Rust base resolver: the graph asked the OS instead of the node that owns it
issues.body:
FOUND 2026-08-16 while closing ISS-123's named remainder ("Resolving the duplicate namespace is
part of closing this").

    packages/tractor/src/main.rs:431      refarm_dir = --refarm-dir | dirs_sovereign_base()
    packages/tractor/src/storage/sqlite.rs:581  db_dir() = XDG_DATA_HOME | ~/.local/share

THE THIRD RUST BASE RESOLVER, after ISS-023 (config_node.rs declared_base) and ISS-050 (storage-fs
scopeRoot), both closed. Same shape every time: a resolver asking the OS instead of reading the
declaration. The daemon is TOLD where its node lives -- --refarm-dir is on its own argv -- and the
graph never consulted it. With XDG_DATA_HOME unset, a SECOND database for the same namespace
appeared silently.

THE EVIDENCE ON THE OPERATOR'S OWN MACHINE, read read-only:

    ~/.refarm/data/refarm/default.db    295KB  2026-08-15 19:46  317 nodes   LIVE
    ~/.local/share/refarm/default.db     48KB  2026-08-05 00:06   21 nodes   ORPHAN

Only 3 of the orphan's 21 ids are also in the live graph. The other 18 are two whole dispatches --
2 UserPrompt, 2 Task, 2 Response, 2 UsageRecord, 2 BudgetObservation -- invisible to the node that
believed it held the record. All token counts are zero, so nothing was spent; what was lost is the
record that they happened. The prompts were probes ("responda apenas: ok" and a file count under
docs/superpowers/specs/).

THE DATE NAMES THE CAUSE. 2026-08-05 is when the sandbox-node slice was being built, and that slice
is the one that DOCUMENTED this behaviour (scripts/refarm-sandbox.mjs:18, "Follows REFARM_HOME? NO").
The leak it wrote down is the leak that produced the file.

FIXED 2026-08-16 in c3f625e4. The chain: XDG_DATA_HOME (still wins -- the sandbox points its graph
at a SIBLING of its REFARM_HOME on purpose, and refarm parity reads declared divergence as healthy)
-> REFARM_HOME/data (exactly what tractor-start.sh:85 derives) -> SOVEREIGN_BASE/SOVEREIGN_DIR/data
-> platform default WITH A WARNING -> refuse. The refusal replaces PathBuf::from("."), which opened
the node's graph relative to whatever directory a shell last cd-ed to.

A TRIPWIRE (orphaned_legacy_graph, pure, existence probe injected) warns when a same-namespace
database sits at the legacy location. It WARNS rather than blocks per ISS-072: the declaration
defect cannot recur, and what remains is a file whose disposition is the operator's call.

THE LIVE NODE DOES NOT MOVE, proven not hoped: the daemon runs with XDG_DATA_HOME=$REFARM_HOME/data
(read from /proc/<pid>/environ), step 1 honours it, and a test pins that precedence.

STILL OPEN, and it is not this item: the orphan FILE itself. 18 nodes exist nowhere else. Discard
with a written rule, or import into the live graph -- the operator decides. Until then `refarm
backup plan` carries both databases, which is the safe direction and is not the same as right.

issues.title: The bundle names which credentials to re-obtain, and three excluded secrets are in no list
issues.body:
FOUND 2026-08-16 by running the instrument for the first time on the operator's real node.
`refarm backup create ~/refarm-backups/2026-08-16` succeeded: state intact, 0 problems, 19 files,
0 undecided, verified against its own manifest.

THE BUNDLE IS HONEST ABOUT WHAT IT CARRIES AND INCOMPLETE ABOUT WHAT IT DOES NOT.

    manifest.reAuthenticate  [cloudflare, github, openai-codex]
    manifest.secrets.files   [.refarm/delivery/telegram.token,
                              .refarm/tls/ca.key,
                              .refarm/tls/serpro-*.key]        included: false

Three secret files are excluded, correctly — carrying them would make the bundle itself a
credential. But NONE of the three is named by `reAuthenticate`, which reads as "here is everything
you must redo". Checked mechanically: no entry of the re-obtain list matches any of the three paths.

WHY IT MATTERS PER FILE, and they are not the same kind of loss:

  - telegram.token   RE-OBTAINABLE from BotFather. Nothing says so, so a restore comes up with
                     delivery silently unable to send.
  - tls/ca.key       NOT RE-OBTAINABLE AT ALL. `refarm cert issue` can create a CA, but it is a
                     NEW one: every device that ran `refarm cert trust` must trust again. That is
                     re-establishment, not re-authentication, and the vocabulary has no word for it.
  - tls/<host>.key   Re-issuable, but only after the CA question above is settled.

THE CLASS: a signal claiming more than it measured — the same family as ISS-113, ISS-124 and
ISS-125. The list is not wrong about what it contains; it is wrong about being the whole answer.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: the excluded secrets each carry their own recovery verb, and the vocabulary
grows a third state beside carried/re-authenticate — something that means RE-ESTABLISH, where the
old value cannot come back and its replacement invalidates trust others already granted. Until
then a restore is partial in a way the manifest does not say.

RELATED: ISS-123 (the capability), ISS-126 (the graph following the declared node).

issues.title: A legacy credential has no identity, so the second login of that provider deletes it and calls it a migration
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-16 against a real SiloCore with SILO_HOME and the catalog home redirected to a

             catalog                 1 descriptor, alias 'segunda', health healthy
             TOKEN-A reachable?      NO — gone from the legacy slot and never written namespaced

THE FIRST ACCOUNT IS LOST BY THE SECOND LOGIN, and the call reports `migratedFromLegacy: true` —
it believes it migrated account A while it deleted A and stored B.

ROOT CAUSE, and it is one function: `legacyDescriptor(provider)`
(packages/model-account-contract-v1/src/migrate.ts:15) takes ONLY the provider. It never opens the
blob. The `accountId` is sitting right there in `oauthCredentials[provider].accountId` and is
ignored; identity is hardcoded `{ status: 'unverified' }`. So `isIndistinguishableAccount` cannot
compare the legacy account against the incoming one — there is nothing to compare — and step 3 of
`account-write.ts` retires the legacy entry BY PROVIDER, assuming it belongs to whoever is logging
in now.

WHY THIS IS NOT ISS-122 REPEATED. ISS-122's mechanism — one slot per provider in the flat map — is
FIXED for the namespaced path, and the operator's own node proves it: two `github-copilot`
accounts, `pessoal` and `corporativo`, both healthy, each with its own envelope. What survives is
the LEGACY-to-new transition, and it survives precisely where the operator is exposed: his
`openai-codex` is still `legacy:oauthCredentials/openai-codex`, and openai-codex is his default
dispatch route.

A GUARD WAS REMOVED ON THE GROUNDS THAT THIS COULD NOT HAPPEN. apps/refarm/src/commands/sow.ts:390
records the interim refusal being deleted in 73692b05: "THE INTERIM REFUSAL IS GONE, and this is
the commit that earns it: it refused a different-account login because the write destroyed the
stored one. The write no longer can." It no longer can from a namespaced account. It still can
from a legacy one.

THE FIX IS SMALL AND IS IN THE PURE PACKAGE: `legacyDescriptor` reads `accountId` from the blob
when present and reports identity accordingly. Then the existing machinery distinguishes A from B,
and step 3 refuses to retire a legacy entry belonging to a different account.

A NOTE ON THE MEASUREMENT ITSELF, because it nearly lied. The first probe read `tokens.secrets`;
`secrets` is a TOP-LEVEL key beside `tokens`, so it reported "0 namespaced envelopes" for a
catalog entry the same run called healthy. Re-read through `silo.listSecrets('model')` and the
count is 1. A probe looking in the wrong place answers "absent" with total confidence.

REPRODUCTION: seed a throwaway silo with a legacy oauthCredentials entry carrying an accountId,
call writeModelCredential for the same provider with a DIFFERENT accountId, then read
silo.listSecrets('model') and the flat map. Hash the operator's real ~/.silo and
~/.refarm/model-accounts.json before and after and fail if either moved.

RELATED: ISS-122 (the umbrella, the namespaced half fixed).

issues.title: The route and the binding decide overlapping things, and nothing reconciles them
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17, in three commands, while running ISS-130's own acceptance on the operator's
real node.

    refarm credential bind refarm model-account:K4NX…   ok
    ~/.refarm/config.json  modelBindings = {
        rcdc5:  model-account:54BG…   (github-copilot, alias pessoal)
        refarm: model-account:K4NX…   (github-copilot, alias corporativo)
    }
    refarm ask --workspace refarm "responda apenas: ok"
      -> "No usable model credentials configured."
    refarm model current --json
      -> rota openai-codex/gpt-5.5, credential state: unresolved

THE BINDING NAMED A COPILOT ACCOUNT AND THE DISPATCH NEVER WENT NEAR IT. The route decided, the
binding did not, and the run failed on a credential belonging to a THIRD provider that no binding
mentions.

## What this actually is

Two axes decide overlapping things and nothing reconciles them:

    route    which PROVIDER and MODEL run   (refarm model use / the route table)
    binding  which ACCOUNT pays             (refarm credential bind, per workspace)

A provider is a protocol and a billing product; an account is one credential-bearing identity
(model-account:v1's own opening sentence). The two axes are correctly SEPARATE — but today they
can name different providers and nothing notices. A binding that says "this workspace spends the
corporate Copilot seat" is silently inert while the route says openai-codex.

That is not a cosmetic disagreement. It is the difference between a declaration and a decoration.

## Why it blocks stated work

The operator's goal is to put idle quota to work — a personal and a CORPORATE Copilot seat — and
to use different demands as the stage for dispatch he can measure across workspaces. ISS-129
measured that Copilot answers the quota question with `limited_user_quotas: null` for both his
SKUs, so the ONLY sovereign depletion signal left is the dispatch outcome. ISS-130 shipped the
attribution that makes such an outcome readable (cdd554de + 2b1945de).

So the instrument is built and there is nothing to instrument: no dispatch can be routed to the
account he wants to observe. The chain is complete except for this link.

## The question, which is a design decision and not a bug report

Does a binding CONSTRAIN the route, or are the axes independent by intent?

  (a) The binding constrains. A workspace bound to a github-copilot account may only dispatch
      through github-copilot; a route naming another provider is a refusal, not a silent
      override. Strongest reading of "declared", and it makes `refarm credential bind` mean what
      an operator plainly assumes it means.
  (b) The axes stay independent and the DISAGREEMENT becomes visible — the route resolves, and
      the node reports that this workspace's binding does not cover the provider about to run,
      leaving the observation unattributed on purpose. Weaker, but preserves a deliberate
      route override.
  NOT (c): the binding quietly picks the route. That would make a per-workspace declaration
      change global dispatch behaviour by a side effect nobody asked for.

Either way the node must stop being able to hold both statements without noticing. The choice is
the operator's, and it decides a contract rather than a field.

## Named beside it, because they surfaced in the same run and are NOT this item

- `openai-codex` is `unresolved` (OPENAI_CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN in neither env nor silo), so even the
  route's own provider cannot dispatch today. A `refarm sow` resolves that and does not touch
  this.
- Both Copilot tokens were expired by 34h/45h with a usable `ghu_` beside them (ISS-129). Nothing
  auto-renews on either provider.

## Acceptance

On the operator's real node: with `refarm` bound to the corporate account, a dispatch either runs
through that account or REFUSES naming the disagreement — never silently spends a different one.
Then `refarm budget by-account --json` returns a non-empty `groups` naming K4NX…, which is also
ISS-130's outstanding acceptance.

RELATED: ISS-130 (attribution, shipped both halves), ISS-129 (Copilot cannot say its quota),
ISS-064 (the denominator).

## OPERATOR RULING 2026-08-17, and it is richer than the two options this item offered

His words, in three tiers plus a rule:

  1. WORKSPACE-SCOPED RUN -> the workspace's binding DRIVES the route.
     Not merely constrains: drives. A run associated with a workspace dispatches through the
     account that workspace is bound to, and the route follows rather than competes. This is
     option (a) of the two offered, taken at its strongest reading.

  2. NODE-LEVEL RUN -> whatever is associated with the NODE decides.
     A dispatch that claims no workspace is not unscoped; it is scoped to the node, and the
     node's own association answers. The tiers do not overlap — each run has exactly one
     scope, and the scope names its authority.

  3. NOTHING ASSOCIATED WITH THE NODE -> the node must DECLARE that, at minimum.
     Either "approved to use everything this node holds", or "approved only for these".

THE THIRD TIER IS THE ONE THIS ITEM DID NOT SEE, and it changes the shape of the answer. It is
not a fallback, it is an AUTHORIZATION. An unbound node must not mean "help yourself to any
credential here" by silence; it must say which it is. Blanket approval is a legitimate answer and
an easy one to give — it just has to be GIVEN, so that a node which never chose is
distinguishable from one that chose everything.

That is the same rule this ledger keeps arriving at from other directions: absence must declare
itself rather than be read as consent. ISS-113 refused a tag no consumer had earned; ISS-125's
doc passed while stale; ISS-128 deleted an account because a legacy blob said nothing about whose
it was. Here silence would spend money.

## What already exists, and what does not — measured 2026-08-17

  EXISTS  the workspace binding — `config.modelBindings`, written by `refarm credential bind`,
          read by `readBindings`. Tier 1 has its data and lacks only the route deferring to it.
  EXISTS, ARGUABLY  the node-level association — `model.routes` (default/worker/monitor) IS what
          is associated with the node today. Tier 2 may need naming rather than building: the
          route table already answers "what does this node run", and the open question is
          whether an account association belongs beside it or replaces it.
  DOES NOT EXIST  the authorization declaration of tier 3. Nothing on this node says whether it
          is approved for all its credentials or only some. Today the answer is implicit and
          therefore unanswerable.

## What this settles and what it opens

SETTLED: (a) over (b). A binding is a declaration and the route follows it for workspace-scoped
runs. The node must never silently spend an account the scope did not name.

OPENED: the authorization surface of tier 3, which is a new contract rather than a field — it
needs a shape, a writer, and a default that is a DECLARATION rather than an absence. Filing that
separately is likely once tier 1 lands, since tier 1 is a route change and tier 3 is a policy
one.

## Acceptance, unchanged in substance and now three-tiered

  workspace-scoped, bound      -> dispatches through the bound account; `budget by-account`
                                  names it.
  node-scoped                  -> dispatches through the node's association, and says so.
  nothing declared anywhere    -> REFUSES, naming that this node has not said what it is
                                  approved to spend — never picks one.

MEASURED WITHOUT SPENDING ANYTHING, 2026-08-17, once `refarm sow` gave the node a resolvable
openai-codex account. `refarm credential current` answers the question this item is about and
answers it locally:

    ~/.refarm/config.json  modelBindings = {
        rcdc5:  model-account:54BG...   github-copilot, alias pessoal
        refarm: model-account:K4NX...   github-copilot, alias corporativo
    }

    refarm credential current --workspace refarm --json
      -> provider: openai-codex, alias: account-2, source: node-default
    refarm credential current --workspace rcdc5 --json
      -> provider: openai-codex, alias: account-2, source: node-default

BOTH BINDINGS ARE INERT. Not overridden by a competing rule — never consulted. The route names
the provider first, and a binding can only disambiguate WITHIN that provider, so a binding to an
account of a different provider has no way to be reached at all.

The earlier evidence in this item read as `unresolved`, which looked like a missing credential
and hid this. It is visible now, and its consequence is the operator_s own axis: work in the
`refarm` workspace spends the openai-codex account while he bound it to the corporate Copilot,
and any per-account budget built on top would be measuring the wrong denominator faithfully.

WHERE TIER 1 LANDS, concretely: the resolver already reports `source`, and `node-default` is the
honest name for what it did. Tier 1 is that a workspace with a binding resolves to that binding_s
PROVIDER as well as its account, and reports `source: workspace-binding`. The seam exists; what
is missing is the precedence.

issues.title: The account view swears a legacy secret is present because it once was
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17 on the operator's node, after `refarm sow` re-authenticated openai-codex.

    ~/.refarm/model-accounts.json   holds  secretRef: legacy:oauthCredentials/openai-codex
    ~/.silo/identity.json           holds  oauthCredentials: {}      <- empty
    refarm credential list          says   health: healthy

A descriptor pointing at a secret that does not exist, reported healthy, and no reconciliation
can ever say otherwise.

`buildAccountView` assembles `merged` from TWO origins — descriptors derived from the flat
tokens in THIS call, and descriptors read from the catalog file — and then declares:

    // Legacy refs are present by definition — their secret is the flat map entry that
    // produced the descriptor
    const presentRefs = [ ...merged.filter(e => e.secretRef.startsWith(LEGACY_REF_PREFIX)) ... ]

The comment states the invariant AND its only justification: the descriptor was produced by
the flat map entry. That is true of the first origin and false of the second. `reconcileCatalog`
is then handed a present-ref list containing refs it was supposed to CHECK, so `healthy` is
stamped on evidence the function invented.

PRESENCE MUST BE DERIVED FROM THE TOKENS ACTUALLY LOADED, not from the shape of the ref. A
legacy ref whose provider is absent from `tokens.oauthCredentials` is `incomplete` — which is
exactly the state the contract already has for 'a descriptor whose secret went missing'.

This is the reader half of the chain that produced ISS-134's wrong sibling count. It does not
create the fossil (see ISS-133); it makes the fossil permanently invisible.

issues.title: `credential forget` writes the derived view back into the catalog
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17. `forget` removes one account and persists the rest:

    const loadAccounts = async () => [...(await deps.viewOf()).accounts];   // the VIEW
    ...
    deps.writeCatalog(accounts.filter((entry) => entry.credentialId !== credentialId));

`accounts` is the reconciled VIEW — catalog descriptors MERGED with descriptors synthesised
from the flat token map by `readLegacyCredentials`. Writing it back into the catalog file
promotes every legacy descriptor from a derived reading into a stored record.

That is CLAUDE.md section 1 in another terrain: the view is a derived observation, the catalog
is the model. Persisting the observation freezes a transient truth — 'the flat map currently
holds openai-codex' — into a permanent one, and the flat map then changes underneath it.

The contract is explicit that this must not happen. `migrate.ts` opens with 'Nothing here
writes... deleting this file restores the old behaviour completely', and `account-view.ts`
defines `legacyAccounts` as the number that says when the transition is over — 'when it is
empty on every node that matters, the legacy branch is deletable'. A persisted legacy
descriptor makes that number never reach zero, because it no longer measures the flat map.

THE FIX IS THE CATALOG, NOT THE VIEW: remove the entry from what `readCatalog` returns and
write that. The view stays the thing commands ANSWER from and stops being the thing they SAVE.

Whether any other write path shares the defect is worth a sweep; today `writeCatalog` has two
callers and the other one (`account-write.ts:110`) upserts onto `readCatalog`, correctly.

issues.title: The migration retires the secret and leaves the record that points at it
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17 — this is what the operator SAW, and the question he asked.

    refarm sow  ->  openai-codex authenticated
                    'This is account 2 of 2 for openai-codex ("account-2").'
                    'Migrated the previous openai-codex credential out of the flat store.'

He has ONE openai-codex account. The node held TWO RECORDS of it and counted records.

The two messages contradict each other and the code knows it. `migratedFromLegacy: true` is
returned ONLY on the branch where `legacySubjectOf(flat[provider]) === accountId` — the node
PROVED the stored credential and the new login are the same account. One line later
`sow.ts:413` counts siblings from the catalog and finds two.

Step 3 retires the flat entry — the SECRET — and leaves any catalog descriptor whose secretRef
is `legacy:oauthCredentials/<provider>`. The module header claims this step is 'what stops a
re-login from producing two accounts for one credential'. It stops half of it.

WHERE THE PROOF ALREADY IS: the same branch that authorises deleting the secret authorises
dropping the record, and nothing else does. Retirement must be one act over both stores, or
the two stores disagree and the disagreement is invisible (ISS-132).

Depends on ISS-133 for how the fossil got into the catalog, and on ISS-132 for why it then
reported healthy. Each is independently a defect; together they cost the operator a phantom
account and an ambiguous dispatch.

ACCEPTANCE: on a node whose flat entry and new login share a subject, after `sow` the catalog
holds exactly one descriptor for that provider, and `credential list` agrees.

issues.title: The select prompt erases a frame it measured at a width that no longer holds
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17. The operator saw the provider picker leave a ghost — the question line and
the first option surviving above a freshly painted frame — while choosing in `refarm sow`.

Reproduced by driving the real prompt against a fake TTY, capturing every byte, and replaying
the stream through a terminal emulator:

    steady width 60,72,80,100,120,160,200    clean
    width unreported (TTY without columns)   clean
    narrowed mid-prompt 120 -> 80            GHOST: question + first option survive
    widened  mid-prompt 80 -> 120            clean

`render()` stores `renderedLines` — physical rows, correctly counted — and the NEXT render
climbs that stored number. The count is measured against `output.columns` at paint time and
trusted at erase time. While the width holds, past and present agree, which is why seven
widths pass. Change the width in between and the number describes a screen that no longer
exists.

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE DANGEROUS PART: widening makes the old frame occupy FEWER rows than
remembered, so the erase rises too far and eats extra — invisible, and therefore absent from
any measurement that only looks for leftovers. Narrowing rises short and leaves the ghost.
Only one of the two failures reports itself.

A previous fix in this same function ('Rows, not lines') corrected HOW the count is computed.
It did not address that the count is REMEMBERED, which is the part that fails here.

TWO HALVES: the frame must record the width it was painted at and refuse to reuse a stale
geometry, and the prompt must repaint on `resize` rather than staying wrongly wrapped until
the next keystroke.

`packages/farm-client/vendor/prompt-contract-v1` is a vendored copy of this file, identical
today, kept aligned by `pnpm --filter @refarm.dev/farm-client run vendor:sync` and guarded by
`vendor:check`. The fix lands in the source and is regenerated, never edited twice.

issues.title: `vendor:check` exists, works, and is wired to nothing
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17, while fixing ISS-135 in `packages/prompt-contract-v1`.

`packages/farm-client/vendor/` holds byte-copies of two packages, and `packages/farm-client`
declares both halves of the mechanism that keeps them true:

    vendor:sync   node scripts/vendor.mjs
    vendor:check  node scripts/vendor.mjs --check

`vendor:check` is referenced by NOTHING — not a workflow, not a lane, not another script. A repo
grep across .github/, package.json and scripts/ returns no caller.

WHAT THAT COST, measured rather than supposed: running `vendor:sync` for the prompt fix also
rewrote `vendor/operation-consent-v1`, whose vendored source was ~500 lines behind its origin —
an entire feature (the outstanding-questions surface on `OperationTrail`) missing from the copy
the farm-client actually loads. Every gate in this repo was green throughout.

This is the same shape as ISS-125 and the requirements-supply audit: the check exists, it works,
and nothing asks it. A guard nobody runs is indistinguishable from one that does not exist, and
worse than none, because its presence reads as coverage.

FIXED IN THE SAME SLICE: `vendor:check` joins the `before-push` repo-contract gates, beside
`validate-packages` and `task:build-order:check`. It belongs there by the lane's own stated rule —
repo-wide rather than change-scoped, and the error escapes the machine rather than the keystroke.
The check is two file comparisons and adds no measurable time.

STILL OPEN: whether CI runs it. The lane's contract is 'say what the pipeline will say', and
the pipeline does not say this yet.
LANDED 2026-08-17 in a7eb6e0d: `vendor:check` is now a `before-push` repo-contract gate,
beside `validate-packages` and `task:build-order:check`, and the ~500-line
`operation-consent-v1` drift it was blind to is paid off in the same commit.

STILL OPEN, which is why this item is: the PIPELINE does not run it. This lane_s stated
contract is to say what the pipeline will say, and right now the lane says more. Until CI
runs the same check, a push from a machine that skipped the lane can still land drift.

## MEASURED 2026-08-23: it is EIGHT gates, not one, and the pipeline has been dark for two weeks

The open half was written as "whether CI runs `vendor:check`". Counted rather than assumed, across
every file in `.github/workflows/`:

    gate                             cost    in any workflow?
    gate-validate-packages           0.6s    yes  (test.yml, validate-scaffold)
    script-organize-imports-test     0.5s    NO
    gate-task-build-order-check      0.6s    NO
    gate-vendor-check                0.5s    NO
    gate-security-audit              6.7s    NO
    gate-rust-test-targets           1.0s    NO
    gate-diagram-sync                0.0s    NO
    gate-script-coverage             0.1s    NO
    gate-script-tests              127.1s    NO

Seven of the eight absent gates cost 9.4s together. The eighth (93 script suites) costs 127s and is
a separate decision. Nothing invokes the lane itself from a workflow, and `quality-gates.yml` is
about `phase:*` PR labels, not these.

## AND THE REASON NONE OF IT SURFACED

The last push to origin/develop was 2026-08-09 (5a9510d3). As of 2026-08-23 the branch is 302
commits ahead. CI has not seen ANY of this work for fourteen days, which is why even the one gate
that IS in a workflow said nothing while it was red.

THREE GATES WERE RED WHEN THIS WAS MEASURED, all introduced 2026-08-19 and all caught only by
running the lane by hand:

  - `validate-packages`  4 packages publishing a `.tsbuildinfo` (9c43fac9) -> fixed f9a19df8
  - `vendor:check`       2 vendored blocks 2 days behind their sources     -> fixed 7604a621
  - `script-coverage`    the closure gate itself shipped with no suite     -> fixed 212f894e

Plus `no-os-resolution`, red since fe4fe3f1 -> fixed a5f8870c. The before-push lane is now green end
to end: 18 steps, 161s.

THE DECISION IS THE OPERATOR'S, because `.github/workflows/**` is a protected surface (AGENTS.md
§8) and because the Actions budget is his: the 9.4s group is nearly free; the 127s one is not.

## CORRECTION 2026-08-23: it is FOUR, not eight — the first count matched the wrong thing

The table above was built by matching each lane STEP ID against the workflow files. Step ids are
not commands. Re-measured by resolving every step through `package.json` to the script it actually
runs, and searching for THAT:

  gate-diagram-sync         -> scripts/check-diagrams.mjs        ALREADY IN CI (validate-diagrams.yml)
  gate-task-build-order     -> scripts/ci/subprocess-utils.mjs   added 652ce162
  gate-script-coverage      -> scripts/script-test-coverage.mjs  added 652ce162
  gate-vendor-check         -> vendor:check                      still absent
  gate-security-audit       -> scripts/security/audit-gate.mjs   still absent
  gate-rust-test-targets    -> scripts/ci/rust-test-targets-gate.mjs   still absent
  gate-script-tests         -> scripts/ci/run-script-tests.mjs   still absent  (132.7s)

`gate-diagram-sync` was never missing; it runs through `validate-diagrams.yml` under the script
name, which the step id does not contain. Recorded because a ledger entry carrying a number nobody
re-derived is the same defect this item is about, one layer up.

WHAT REMAINS, with what each needs — measured in a dependency-free worktree, which is what a fresh
CI job is:

  vendor:check          needs the workspace; BUILDS the block when dist is absent (by design:
                        "a drift check that quietly passes when it cannot look is not a check")
  audit-gate.mjs        needs pnpm + network. CI HAS an `audit-moderate` job at the same scope —
                        and it is explicitly NON-BLOCKING, while the operator's 2026-08-11 ruling
                        is that `moderate --prod` with per-advisory expiry IS the promotion gate.
                        Making it blocking can break the pipeline; that is ISS-088's own framing
                        and remains his call.
  rust-test-targets     ran past 2 MINUTES in a cold worktree. The 0.7s local figure was a warm
                        cargo cache, and quoting it as a CI cost would have been wrong.
  run-script-tests      132.7s. Belongs in the weekly Release Health, not in every push: at ~176
