issues.title: Seven packages named `*-contract-v1` are validated as `buildable`, and nothing says so
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17, from the operator's question: can the scaffold help us keep what we
generate coherent?

`pnpm validate-packages` ends with 'All packages conform to their scaffold type.' It is true,
and it is not the sentence it appears to be. Of 36 packages named `*-contract-v1`:

    contract-v1              24
    structural-contract-v1    5
    buildable                 7   <- history, lab, model-account, node, pressure,
                                     prompt, workspace-access

THE NAME IS A DECLARATION AND NOTHING CHECKS IT AGAINST THE SHAPE. A package that declares
itself a contract and does not carry a contract's obligations is not reported — it is
silently classified as the weaker type and validated against those rules instead. The gate
then passes, honestly, having asked a different question than the one its output implies.

## Two distinct causes, and they want different repairs

1. THE CLASSIFIER KEYS ON A FILENAME. `contract-v1` requires `src/conformance.ts` to exist.
   `prompt-contract-v1` ships a full conformance suite — `runOperatorChannelConformance`,
   exported from `index.ts`, with a `test:conformance` script wired to it — and is demoted
   anyway, because the code is not in a file with that name. `history` and `pressure` also
   declare `test:conformance`. The classifier is detecting a filename; the property it means
   to detect is a capability.

2. FOUR CARRY NO CONFORMANCE AT ALL: lab, model-account, node, workspace-access. That is a
   real gap rather than a detection miss, and `model-account-contract-v1` is the one that
   costs most right now — every credential resolution rule this repo has, including the
   precedence changed today for ISS-131 and the quota reading added for ISS-064, lives in a
   package validated as an ordinary buildable library.

## The generator's side of the operator's question

`turbo/generators` has a `contract-v1` template (`types.ts`, `conformance.ts`, `in-memory.ts`,
`index.ts`) and it CANNOT help the four: they already exist, and a generator only speaks at
creation. This is exactly the asymmetry worth naming — the scaffold is enforced at birth and
never again, so a package can only drift away from its type, never back.

## What lands now, and what does not

A RATCHET, not a red gate. Blocking outright would fail seven packages at once for a
condition none of their authors were told about, which is the opposite of ISS-072's rule
that a gate blocks only what the agent can fix. So: the seven are recorded with the date and
the reason, an eighth fails, and the number can only go down.

NOT LANDING, and deliberately: writing conformance suites for the four. A conformance suite
in this repo is 'the checks, as data, so a Rust or WASM implementation runs the same list'
— it earns its place when a second implementation exists. Writing one speculatively would
produce a file that satisfies the classifier and asserts nothing anybody depends on, which
is the exact failure this item is about, arriving from the other direction.

issues.title: The readiness gate reads the store `sow` migrates AWAY from, so a fully migrated node reports no credentials
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17 on the operator's node, immediately after `refarm sow` succeeded:

    refarm credential list   -> 3 accounts, all healthy
    refarm ask --workspace refarm 'responda apenas: ok'
      -> No usable model credentials configured.
         Set up credentials: refarm sow

It sent him to run the command he had just run.

`detectProvider` gathers evidence from four sources — env, `.env`, `identity.json`,
`config.json` — and every one of them reads the FLAT credential shape. `sow` writes the
secret into Silo's `model` namespace and RETIRES the flat entry, which is the entire point
of the namespaced store. So `identity.json` still declares `modelProvider: openai-codex`,
the flat map beside it is `{}`, and the gate resolves `declared-missing`.

THE MORE COMPLETELY A NODE MIGRATES, THE MORE CERTAIN THIS GATE BECOMES THAT IT HAS NOTHING.
That is the shape worth naming: it is not a gate that fails on a broken node, it is one that
fails on a finished one.

THIRD READER IN THE SAME FAMILY this week. ISS-132 was the account view swearing a legacy ref
was present because of its shape; this is the readiness gate; ISS-140 is the runtime's
credential injection. Each was written when the flat map was the only store, each is correct
about what it reads, and none was told the store moved.

FIXED: `catalogEvidence` — a `healthy` descriptor in the catalog is a usable credential. Only
`healthy` counts; an `incomplete` descriptor is a login that happened and a secret that did
not survive, and treating it as evidence would turn a fail-closed gate into one that passes
on intent. It yields `none` rather than `declared-missing` when the catalog holds nothing, so
an empty catalog cannot veto a source that does have a working credential.

issues.title: `home` meant two different directories in the account store, and one caller silently read nothing
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17, while making the workspace binding drive the route (ISS-131). The route
did not change, and the reason was not the route:

    resolveRefarmHome()        = /home/.../.refarm
    readBindings(refarmHome)   -> []          <- reads .refarm/.refarm/config.json
    readCatalog(refarmHome)    -> 0 entries
    readBindings($HOME)        -> 2 bindings
    readCatalog($HOME)         -> 3 entries

`CATALOG_FILE` carried the `.refarm/` segment, so `home` meant THE DIRECTORY CONTAINING the
refarm home. `credential.ts` and `sow.ts` passed `process.env.HOME` and were right;
`ask.ts` passed `resolveRefarmHome()` and was wrong. Both are strings, both compile, and the
wrong one returns an EMPTY LIST rather than throwing.

WHAT IT COST, and it is the answer to a question that was open for a day: ISS-130 shipped the
`credentialId` stamp on every dispatch, and `refarm budget by-account` kept reporting
`groups: 0 / unattributed: 32`. The stamp was reading bindings from a path that does not
exist. It was never firing. The write side was correct and the read beneath it was silent.

A SECOND, LATENT BUG IN THE SAME CONSTANT: `$HOME + .refarm/` ignores a declared
`REFARM_HOME`. A node with a redirected home kept its accounts under the operator's real
`$HOME` — invisible until someone redirected one.

FIXED by giving `home` ONE meaning: the REFARM HOME, which is what `resolveRefarmHome()`
answers and what every modern reader in this repo already uses (`model-rate-catalog.ts`
joins filenames onto it directly). `CATALOG_FILE` is now a basename, `readBindings` joins
`config.json` directly, and `credential.ts`/`sow.ts` pass the declared home. The operator's
files do not move: with `REFARM_HOME` unset both readings resolve to the same path.

issues.title: The runtime is provisioned from the flat token map, so it can serve only the provider it booted with
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17, as the last wall between the operator and a dispatch that spends the
account he bound. With ISS-131 tier 1 landed the CLI routes correctly, and:

    refarm ask --workspace refarm 'responda apenas: ok'
      Agent turn — route github-copilot (override)
      [blocked: model-bridge provider mismatch: requested 'github-copilot',
       expected 'openai-codex']

## The guard is right; it was told the wrong thing

`wasi_bridge/core.rs` enforces an EGRESS ALLOWLIST: the guest may reach the primary route,
an optional fallback, and every route named in `MODEL_CONFIGURED_PROVIDERS`. That last one
exists for exactly this — 'the routes a routing profile may legitimately select ... so a
profile can pick AMONG the operator's configured providers'. Nothing in the host needs to
change. It was simply never told the node has two providers.

## Two readers, both blind to the namespaced store

1. `configuredProviders(env)` derives the list from WHICH CREDENTIAL ENV VARS ARE PRESENT.
   The operator's credentials live in Silo's `model` namespace, so no env var is set, so
   the list is empty and the host accepts only the boot route.
2. `credentialLocationFor` resolves through `readLegacyCredentials(tokens)` — the FLAT map
   only. After `sow` migrates a provider out, this finds nothing to inject at all.

THE DISPATCH THAT WORKS TODAY IS WORKING ON A STALE ENV. The runtime is a daemon; its
openai-codex credential was injected before the migration and survives in its process
environment. Nothing would re-inject it after a restart. This is a node one `runtime
restart` away from having no model at all, and it would then report the ISS-138 message.

## What this needs, and why it is not landed in the same slice

Provisioning the runtime from the CATALOG rather than the flat map is the fix, and it
carries a POSTURE DECISION that is the operator's: how many credentials should live in the
runtime's environment at once. Injecting every healthy account widens what a compromised
guest can reach; injecting only the bound one means a node cannot serve two workspaces
without a restart. `packages/tractor/**` is a protected surface and this touches what it
guards, even though the change itself is in `apps/farmhand`.

THE THIRD TIER OF ISS-131 IS THE SAME QUESTION FROM THE OTHER SIDE. The operator ruled that
a node with nothing associated must DECLARE what it is authorised to spend. The set of
credentials the runtime is provisioned with is that declaration made operational — which
suggests the two want one answer rather than two.

## CORRECTED 2026-08-17. The posture paragraph above states the risk wrongly.

It says injecting every healthy account 'widens what a compromised guest can reach'. It does
not. Measured in `wasi_bridge/core.rs`: the HOST makes the HTTP call and reads the API key from
its own process env at send time, keyed off the provider; the guest calls the bridge with
(provider, base_url, path, body) and never holds a key. `configured-providers-env.ts` states the
same rule from the other side — the env-forward gate blocks secret-shaped vars from reaching a
plugin, which is why a non-secret NAME list had to be invented in the first place.

THE RISK IS SPEND, NOT EXFILTRATION. A misbehaving guest cannot read a credential; it can ask
the host to POST to any provider on the allowlist, and the host will attach that provider's key.
That is the CONFUSED DEPUTY, exactly, and naming it correctly changes what the fix must do:
protecting the key is already done, and bounding what may be SPENT is not.

## The shape refarm already has, named

This is the credential-broker pattern that agent security has converged on, and refarm arrived at
it independently. Mapped onto the IETF CB4A draft (draft-hartman-credential-broker-4-agents-00):

    CDP (holds credentials, mints/attaches)   = the tractor host, keys in its process env
    Agent (never holds a credential)          = the WASM guest, holds a bridge handle
    Policy                                    = the egress allowlist: primary + fallback +
                                                MODEL_CONFIGURED_PROVIDERS

WHERE IT DIVERGES, and this is the part worth acting on:

  - CB4A: tokens are TASK-SCOPED and non-renewable; each task re-attests.
    refarm: all three route sets resolve ONCE AT PLUGIN LOAD. The allowlist is per-daemon.
  - CB4A: 'Enforce broker mediation through firewall rules and DNS controls, NOT agent
    cooperation.' refarm: with a union allowlist, which account a task spends is decided by the
    CLI — a cooperating component — and the host would accept any of them.
  - CB4A: 'the justification is auditable evidence, NOT an authorization input.' Here the
    workspace binding is the CLI's justification, and the host has no policy of its own to check
    it against, so it takes it on faith.

## Why the industry answer does not transfer directly

LLM gateways (LiteLLM and peers) solve the identical multi-account/multi-budget problem with
VIRTUAL KEYS: one revocable, budgeted credential per team, so a leak costs one budget rather than
the provider account. That answer is unavailable here — a Copilot seat and a ChatGPT subscription
issue no sub-credentials. There is nothing to hand out per workspace.

WHICH IS PRECISELY WHY THE ALLOWLIST HAS TO CARRY THE AUTHORIZATION. Where a gateway would
express the boundary as a key, this node can only express it as a declaration. That makes ISS-131
tier 3 and this item ONE object seen from two sides: what the node declares it is authorised to
spend IS what the host is provisioned with.

## What must not be done, stated so it is not done later by accident

Deriving `MODEL_CONFIGURED_PROVIDERS` from 'every healthy account' unblocks today and makes the
budget record UNFALSIFIABLE: every account is spendable on every task, the binding becomes
advisory, and `refarm budget by-account` reports which account was DECLARED to have paid with
nothing having enforced it. A routing bug and a compromise would then look identical in the
record — and the record is the only durable output this node has.

## PARTIALLY CLOSED 2026-08-17 — the declaration now provisions the runtime.

`MODEL_CONFIGURED_PROVIDERS` is derived from `modelAuthorization` rather than from which
credential env vars happen to exist, the credentials of every authorised provider are exported
(not only the route's), and their endpoints travel with them. The runtime is no longer
provisioned from the flat token map.

STILL OPEN, and it is the tier the operator deferred: the host resolves its allowlist ONCE AT
PLUGIN LOAD, so which account a task spends is still decided by the CLI. The declaration bounds
WHAT the node may spend; nothing yet bounds what a single task may.

One credential env var per provider is what makes that gap load-bearing rather than theoretical:
two authorised accounts of one provider cannot both be provisioned, so `provisionableAccounts`
refuses and names the collision. Authorising exactly one account per provider is what makes a
multi-account node serviceable TODAY — and per-task scoping is what would let the operator stop
choosing.

## TIER B LANDED 2026-08-17. The host now bounds the TASK.

`routes_for_task` intersects the boot allowlist with what the invocation declared, and the
runner sets that declaration before the guest runs and clears it after. Verified live: a
node-level dispatch narrows to openai-codex and answers; a workspace-scoped one narrows to
github-copilot and reaches Copilot_s own API.

THREE PROPERTIES CARRY IT, and each was chosen against a specific way of being wrong:

  - MONOTONIC. Narrowing can only intersect, never widen, which is what makes reading the
    task_s own declaration sound. Authorization still comes from the node_s declaration; only
    SELECTION comes from the task.
  - EMPTY IS A REFUSAL. A task naming an unauthorised provider is refused, not served by the
    primary route. The silent substitution is the defect itself.
  - FAILS TOWARD THE PREVIOUS BEHAVIOUR. An unparseable payload yields no narrowing and the
    node-wide set stands; refusing on unfamiliar JSON would make an unrelated payload change
    break every model call.

NO LOCK, AND NOT BY LUCK: a plugin_s invocations are served by one task that owns the handle and
calls the guest one at a time. Measured in `lib.rs` before the design relied on it.

## What this unlocks, and what it does not

The one-credential-per-provider wall STANDS: the host still reads one credential env var per
provider, so two authorised accounts of one provider still cannot both be provisioned and
`provisionableAccounts` still refuses and names the collision. Tier B bounds WHERE a task may
send, not WHICH of two same-provider seats pays.

Closing that would mean the credential travelling with the task rather than living in the
process environment — a different and larger change, and the first one that would need the host
to hold more than one secret per provider at a time.

## CLOSED 2026-08-20 — proven on the operator's node, and the last STILL OPEN above was stale.

The section titled "The one-credential-per-provider wall STANDS" argued against code that had
already changed: ISS-145 landed the day after it was written and moved the credential onto the
task. This is the fourth item in this repository to do that, and it is why the acceptance below
is a live measurement rather than a re-reading.

WHAT THE NODE ACTUALLY HAS (measured, live runtime, 2.7h uptime):

    MODEL_CONFIGURED_PROVIDERS = github-copilot,openai-codex
    MODEL_ACCOUNT_CREDENTIALS  = 3 credentials, keyed by opaque id
    MODEL_ACCOUNT_CREDENTIALS_PATH = ~/.refarm/model-accounts.token (3, same ids)

    model-account:54BG…  github-copilot  pessoal      https://api.individual.githubcopilot.com
    model-account:K4NX…  github-copilot  corporativo  https://api.business.githubcopilot.com
    model-account:3WGF…  openai-codex    account-2

Both Copilot seats provisioned at once, with DIFFERENT endpoints — the exact pair this item said
could never coexist.

ACCEPTANCE, end to end:

    refarm ask --workspace rcdc5  'responda apenas: ok'
      -> Agent turn — route github-copilot (override)
      -> ok    (model gpt-4o, 2141 in / 3 out, subscription)

    refarm ask --workspace refarm 'responda apenas: ok'
      -> refused: quota. NOT a routing failure — the corporate seat reached its own endpoint and
         that seat has 0/10000 premium_interactions remaining (measured below).

FALSIFIABLE, which this item required of itself ("the record is the only durable output"):

    refarm budget by-account
      model-account:54BG…   20 observations   29431 in / 42 out
      model-account:K4NX…   17 observations    7309 in / 12 out
      unattributed          36 observations   (historical, ISS-073)

Bind -> dispatch -> the bound seat pays -> the record names which. Nothing here is taken on faith.

## WHAT THE PROOF REVEALED, and it is the sustainability axis rather than this item

    refarm credential quota
      pessoal      individual  premium_interactions 1500/1500   chat unlimited  completions unlimited
      corporativo  business    premium_interactions    0/10000  chat unlimited  completions unlimited
      openai-codex             cannot-ask

The node holds 1500 idle premium interactions on one seat and 0 on another, and a workspace bound
to the exhausted one is told only "Model quota or billing limit reached". It does not say which
METER is exhausted, with what numbers, resetting when, nor that another authorised seat has room.
Two facts the node already reads and does not carry into the refusal.

NOT AUTOMATIC FAILOVER. The personal/corporate frontier is the operator's, and a node that
silently spends a personal seat for corporate work has crossed it without being asked. The gap is
INFORMATION, not policy — and it is the same shape as `credential quota`'s third state: say
exactly what is known, and leave the decision where it belongs.

Carried to its own item rather than reopening this one.

issues.title: github-copilot can be logged in, read and measured — and never dispatched: no route in host or guest
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17, at the end of the chain that was supposed to make the operator's corporate
Copilot seat spendable. Every layer above it now works:

    refarm credential authorize K4NX… 3WGF…      declared
    MODEL_CONFIGURED_PROVIDERS=github-copilot,openai-codex
    GITHUB_COPILOT_ACCESS_TOKEN exported          yes
    refarm credential current --workspace refarm  github-copilot / corporativo / workspace-binding
    refarm ask --workspace refarm                 route github-copilot (override)
      -> Model provider unavailable: ollama

## github-copilot has no DISPATCH route, in either half of the runtime

    packages/agent/src/provider_config.rs   openai_compat_defaults() has no copilot arm
                                            `_ => ("http://localhost:11434", "llama3.2")`
    packages/tractor/.../core.rs            known_provider_base_url() has no copilot entry
                                            for_provider() falls to the same localhost floor

So a dispatch routed to github-copilot resolves to OLLAMA, on both sides, and the error names
ollama for a request nobody made to ollama. Nothing is broken; the provider was never wired for
dispatch.

## What shipped was the LOGIN, not the dispatch

This is worth stating plainly because the node's own record says otherwise. `sow` authenticates
Copilot, two accounts coexist healthy, `credential list` names them, identity is verified, and
`refarm credential quota` reads real per-seat numbers from GitHub. Every one of those is
credential handling. None of them sends a completion.

## Four pieces, and the fourth is not the one anybody expects

1. GUEST: a `github-copilot` arm in `openai_compat_defaults` (base url + default model).
2. HOST: a `known_provider_base_url` entry, so the egress allowlist admits the real endpoint
   rather than the localhost floor. `packages/tractor/**` is a protected surface.
3. HEADERS: Copilot requires editor-identity headers alongside the bearer token; the generic
   arm sends `authorization` only. The node already declares this imitation openly via
   `providers.githubCopilot.identity`, so the choice is made — it just is not made HERE.
4. RENEWAL IS A DIFFERENT MECHANISM. The stored `access` is a SHORT-LIVED copilot token (`tid=`
   prefix) obtained by exchanging the `ghu_`; it is not renewed by an OAuth `refresh_token`
   grant, so `OAUTH_TOKEN_URLS`/`OAUTH_CLIENT_IDS` cannot carry it and github-copilot is absent
   from both. The exchange is `GET https://api.github.com/copilot_internal/v2/token` with the
   `ghu_`, which `apps/refarm/src/credentials/copilot-quota.ts` already performs for quota —
   the same call, read for a different field.

## The base url is per-ACCOUNT, which is the part that will bite

The token exchange returns the endpoint (`proxy-ep`), and the stored credential records it as
`baseUrl` with `baseUrlSource: from-token`. A static table entry is therefore a DEFAULT, not the
truth: the host resolves one base url at boot, so two Copilot accounts whose exchanges return
different endpoints cannot both be served by one daemon. That is the same wall as ISS-140's
one-credential-per-provider, arriving through the endpoint instead of the key, and it says the
per-task route scoping is not optional for this provider — it is what makes it work at all.

## Until then

The operator's corporate seat is READABLE (quota, identity, health) and not SPENDABLE. Binding a
workspace to it now produces an honest failure rather than a wrong charge, which is the right
order for those two to arrive in.

## THE ADAPTER LANDED 2026-08-17, and the dispatch reached Copilot.

    refarm ask --workspace refarm 'responda apenas: ok'
      Agent turn — route github-copilot (override)
      HTTP 401: IDE token expired: unauthorized: token expired

That 401 is COPILOT'S OWN API answering. Route, allowlist, per-account endpoint, path and
editor headers all worked — the request arrived and was refused for the age of its token. The
four pieces this item named are built:

  1. guest `openai_compat_defaults` arm + `request_path` arm (`/chat/completions`, no `/v1`)
  2. host `known_provider_api_path` arm and a PER-PROVIDER endpoint map
  3. the editor-identity headers, and `GITHUB_COPILOT_ACCESS_TOKEN` as the credential var the
     host reads (it derived `GITHUB_COPILOT_API_KEY`, which nothing writes)
  4. the re-exchange renewal, in the CLI that provisions the runtime and in the daemon

### The endpoint could not be a table, and that is now proven rather than argued

`MODEL_PROVIDER_BASE_URLS` carries `provider=url` pairs, written by the CLI from each authorised
account's own credential and parsed IDENTICALLY by host and guest. The lockstep is the point: the
host validates every request against its own resolution, so a guest that read the map differently
would build requests the host refuses.

### Two defects found on the way, both fixed

  - the guest sent `/v1/chat/completions` where Copilot serves `/chat/completions`
  - `enforce_model_route_any` surfaced the PRIMARY route's complaint even when a configured route
    had been admitted for that very provider and refused it for another reason. A Copilot request
    rejected for its PATH was reported as `provider mismatch: requested 'github-copilot',
    expected 'openai-codex'` — a question nobody asked, and it sent the search at the allowlist
    while the real difference was one path segment. It now reports the NEAREST route's complaint.

## WHAT REMAINS IS NOT CODE — GitHub refuses the exchange

Measured, both of the operator's accounts, interleaved with the sibling path on the same token:

    /copilot_internal/user      -> 200  server: github.com  application/json
    /copilot_internal/v2/token  -> 403  server: (absent)    text/html    4/4 consistent

An `x-github-request-id` IS present on the 403, so the request reaches GitHub's edge — this is a
refusal, not the corporate network, and not the 502/503 intermittency measured earlier (which is
real and separate: ~25% on this network, on both paths). It happens with refarm's own identity
and with the declared editor imitation, with `Bearer` and with `token`, on the personal seat and
the corporate one — so it is not an organisation policy either.

The operator's stored credentials carry `baseUrlSource: from-token`, so an exchange DID succeed
at login on 2026-08-16. Either the `ghu_` tokens have aged out of their Copilot authorization or
GitHub tightened the endpoint since.

THE NEXT MOVE IS AN OPERATOR ACTION: `refarm sow` re-authenticates through the device flow,
which mints a fresh `ghu_` and a live Copilot token in the same act. Every layer beneath that is
now proven, so the dispatch should complete on the first try after it — and if the exchange 403s
during the login too, that is the same wall arriving where it can actually be seen.

NOT A REASON TO WEAKEN THE RENEWAL. It fails closed: an exchange that does not answer 200 leaves
the stored credential exactly as it was and the request that follows says what the provider
thinks of it. A renewal that deleted or replaced a credential on a refused exchange would have
turned this measurement into a lost account.

## CORRECTED 2026-08-17, and the correction is the lesson.

The section above concludes that GitHub refuses this client, and offers two explanations: the
`ghu_` tokens aged out, or GitHub tightened the endpoint. BOTH ARE WRONG. GitHub was in a
declared incident at the moment of every one of those measurements:

    Incident with GitHub.com — critical, since 13:40 UTC 2026-08-17
      Copilot ......... major_outage
      API Requests .... operational
    18:11  residual impact in the form of sporadic authentication failures
    19:13  we have partially disabled authentication token retries

`copilot_internal/v2/token` IS an authentication token exchange. The probes ran 19:0x-19:5x.

THE MEASUREMENT WAS RIGHT AND THE CONCLUSION OVER-REACHED. 403 four times out of four, two
accounts, two identities, request-id present — all true, and none of it licensed the leap to
which SIDE was at fault, because the provider was never asked whether it was healthy. The status
page is a free, decisive input that went unconsulted. This is the same shape as ISS-129, which
this very slice had corrected an hour earlier: measure one thing thoroughly, then widen the
conclusion past what the measurement covers.

It also explains the 401 that started this: the operator_s token expired and could not be renewed
because the exchange had been down since 13:40.

## What that cost him, and what now prevents it

refarm_s own error said the endpoint may only honour known integration ids — true as a possible
cause, read as a diagnosis. He re-registered an identity, re-ran the device flow three times and
set a config key that was already set. `provider-status.ts` now answers first, in three states,
and the identity hint appears only in the world where it is still the right suspicion.

## The adapter is unblocked, pending the incident

Nothing in the adapter is waiting on a change. When Copilot_s auth is restored, `refarm sow`
mints a live token and the dispatch that already reached Copilot completes.

issues.title: The GitHub Copilot wire is parked in the generic account contract; it wants its own provider block
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17, and prompted by the operator's own note mid-slice: evaluate where things
best live, for the sake of cultivating the general SDK.

Making GitHub Copilot dispatchable (ISS-141) needed its undocumented wire in TWO apps — the CLI
provisions the runtime, the daemon renews mid-run, and `apps/farmhand` cannot import from
`apps/refarm`. The wire moved into `@refarm.dev/model-account-contract-v1` as a WAYPOINT, which
is where it should not stay.

## The line, and it is a clean one

    GENERIC (stays in the account contract)     PROVIDER (belongs elsewhere)
    descriptors, health, resolution             the copilot token exchange url + headers
    bindings, authorization, precedence         parsing a copilot token's fields
    QuotaMeter / AccountQuota vocabulary        deriving the per-seat endpoint from it
    isMeterExhausted, meteredEntries            reading `quota_snapshots` into meters
    provisionableAccounts                       the identity profiles refarm may present

VOCABULARY IS GENERIC, PARSING IS PER PROVIDER. `readQuotaMeter` reads `unlimited`,
`has_quota`, `percent_remaining` — Copilot's field names — while the three states it produces
are provider-neutral and already carry the trap worth keeping generic (an unlimited meter
reporting `remaining: 0`).

## Why it matters beyond tidiness

ISS-137 measured seven packages whose NAME declares a contract and whose shape does not, and the
repair for four of them is genuine. Letting one provider's undocumented wire settle into the
generic account contract is that drift arriving from the other direction — the package would
still be named a contract and would increasingly be a provider adapter.

NAMED FOR WHAT IT IS: `@refarm.dev/github-copilot-wire`, NOT `*-contract-v1`. It is an adapter
for one provider's undocumented surface, it has no conformance suite to offer, and naming it a
contract would trip the ratchet ISS-137 just planted — correctly.

## Not done in the same slice, deliberately

A new package is a scaffold plus two hand-maintained registries plus a full gate run, at the end
of a slice that already rebuilt the WASM component and the runtime. The extraction is mechanical
and provable — tests green on both sides of a move that changes no behaviour — which is exactly
the kind of change that should own its own commit and its own green tree.

issues.title: GitHub Models is retired and a GitHub App is not a dispatch path — the map, so nobody re-derives it
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17, chasing the operator's question: if the Copilot editor door is stuck,
can we prepare a GitHub App instead?

The answer is that the documented door was already closed before we looked at it.

## GitHub Models is retired

    GET https://models.github.ai/catalog/models
      410  {"error":{"code":"github_models_retirement_brownout",
            "message":"GitHub Models is temporarily unavailable as part of a scheduled
            retirement brownout."}}

Announced 2026-07-01, fully retired 2026-07-30 — playground, catalog, inference API and
bring-your-own-key, for every customer including existing ones. That was 18 days before this
measurement. The 410 body still says 'brownout', which is the retirement's own leftover wording
and would have read as a temporary condition to anybody who did not check the date.

IT WAS THE RIGHT SHAPE, and that is why losing it matters: OpenAI-compatible
`POST /inference/chat/completions`, authenticated by a fine-grained PAT with `models:read` OR BY
A GITHUB APP, with an org-scoped variant `POST /orgs/{org}/inference/chat/completions` that
ATTRIBUTED INFERENCE TO THE ORGANISATION. Documented, supported, no impersonation, and per-org
attribution that maps onto this node's workspace/cost axis almost exactly.

## What that leaves

GitHub's own migration guidance points back at Copilot for model access on GitHub. So the
undocumented editor endpoint refarm already speaks is not a shortcut around a documented
alternative — since 2026-07-30 there is no documented alternative to be around.

THE GITHUB APP IS NOT A DISPATCH PATH TODAY. GitHub's incident note during the outage said
'Copilot usage via the GitHub CLI and GitHub App are unaffected', which reads like a door: it is
not one for us. A GitHub App reaches Copilot as an EXTENSION — GitHub calls the app — which is
the inverse direction from a node dispatching its own work. Building one would not produce a
credential this runtime can spend.

## Why this is filed rather than acted on

Nothing here is a defect and nothing is buildable. It is the map: two of the three doors an
operator would reasonably try are closed, and the reasons are dated and public. Without it
written down, the next slice that asks 'why not just use GitHub Models / a GitHub App' spends a
day rediscovering a retirement announcement and an inverse-direction API.

WORTH RE-CHECKING IF: GitHub ships a successor inference API, or Copilot Extensions gain an
outbound completion surface. Neither is announced.

issues.title: A model id survived a change of provider, so the route named a model the provider does not serve
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17 on the operator's node, and it is the last thing that stood between him and
a working Copilot dispatch.

He re-authenticated GitHub Copilot. `sow` wrote `modelProvider: github-copilot` and left
`modelId: gpt-5.5` — openai-codex's model — so the node's route became:

    current:  github-copilot/gpt-5.5      <- provider of one, model of another
    routes:   worker  -> github-copilot/gpt-4o
              monitor -> github-copilot/gpt-4o

and the first dispatch through it reached Copilot and was refused by Copilot's own API:

    HTTP 400  model "gpt-5.5" is not accessible via the /chat/completions endpoint

## Derived followed its owner; pinned did not

The scoped routes were RIGHT the whole time, and that is the diagnosis rather than a detail:
`worker` and `monitor` are derived from the provider, so they moved with it. `modelId` is a PIN,
and a pin outlives whatever it was pinned to unless something re-derives it.

The same shape as the Copilot base url being per-account (ISS-141): a value that belongs to one
thing, stored beside another, surviving a change of the first.

## The rule, and its two refusals

`modelIdForProviderChange` re-derives the pin when the provider MOVED, and does nothing when:

  - the provider is UNCHANGED — a re-login must not silently replace a model the operator chose
  - there was NO pin — writing one would pin something he never chose, and the route already
    derives correctly without it

## Found on the way: ISS-140 tier B shipped INERT

`declared_model_provider` read `modelProvider` at the top level of the dispatch payload. The wire
carries `provider`: the CLI writes `args.provider`, `dispatch.rs` copies it into the payload, and
the guest reads `provider`. Nothing sends the name I read, so the per-task narrowing never fired
— and a guard that cannot fire reports the same silence as one with nothing to catch. Fixed in
the same commit, with the other spellings kept as a hedge that costs nothing.

## Verified end to end after both fixes

    refarm ask --workspace refarm 'responda apenas: ok'
      route github-copilot (override)  ->  ok
      model: gpt-4o   tokens: 1814 in / 3 out   subscription
    refarm budget by-account  ->  model-account:...39VN67PR  obs=9  in=1814  out=3

The workspace binding chose the account, the host narrowed to it, Copilot served it, and the
record attributes the spend to the seat that paid. That is ISS-130's acceptance with real tokens
rather than a blocked dispatch's zeros.

issues.title: One provider could hold only one spendable seat, because the credential lived in the process and not on the task
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-17. The wall ISS-140 tier B named and did not move: the host bounds WHERE a
task may send, and nothing bounded WHICH SEAT pays when one provider holds two.

    bearer_key_for_provider(provider) -> one env var per provider

So the operator's personal and corporate Copilot seats — different endpoints, different
entitlements — could never both be provisioned. `provisionableAccounts` refused the pair and
made him authorise one, and a workspace bound to the other could not be honoured.

## Keyed by the id everything else already uses

`MODEL_ACCOUNT_CREDENTIALS` carries every authorised seat by OPAQUE credential id — what the
dispatch declares and what the budget observation stamps. The seat that was bound, the seat that
pays and the seat the record names become ONE id rather than three inferences that can disagree.

IT NEVER REACHES A PLUGIN, refused BY NAME in the env-forward policy and pinned by a test there.
A name that merely happened not to match the `*_KEY` / `*_TOKEN` patterns would have forwarded
live tokens to a guest, which is the one failure that policy exists to make impossible.

THE ENDPOINT TRAVELS WITH THE SEAT for the same reason the key does: Copilot's exchange announces
a different host per seat, so a per-provider map cannot hold both. Precedence, narrowest first:
the task's seat, then the provider map, then the global override, then the static default.

## Verified live, both seats of one provider on one node

    ask --workspace refarm  -> corporate seat  -> ok   1814 in / 3 out
    ask --workspace rcdc5   -> personal seat   -> ok   1814 in / 3 out
    budget by-account       -> 2 groups, separate spend

## Three defects found by live failure, and what each taught

1. THE RENEWAL SKIPPED EXACTLY THE ACCOUNTS IT WAS FOR. It iterated `provisionableAccounts`,
   which refuses a provider holding two authorised seats — so authorising both Copilot accounts
   stopped either from being renewed, and both expired. A renewal that runs only where it was
   not needed.

2. THE NARROWING WAS WIRED INTO ONE OF TWO DISPATCH SHAPES. `refarm ask` fires a reply-LESS
   envelope served by `on_event`; only `respond` had it. On the operator's note about
   centralising common failure points, both now call ONE `set_task_scope` that owns the parsing
   AND both writes — a third dispatch shape cannot half-adopt it. This is the second time in two
   slices that a guard shipped inert and nothing said so.

3. `base_url not allowed` NAMED NEITHER URL. It sent the search at the allowlist while the
   difference was one seat's endpoint against another's. Both are printed now; they are
   addresses, not credentials.

## What this does not do

The per-provider env vars remain as the fallback for a dispatch that declares no seat, which is
every node-level run and every un-bound workspace. Nothing about the previous behaviour changed
for them.

issues.title: The lint never reads Rust test targets, so an integration test that stopped compiling was invisible
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-18. `tractor-rs:lint` runs `cargo clippy` WITHOUT `--all-targets`, and
`test --lib` does not reach integration tests either — they are separate binaries. So
`tests/source_provider_sidecar_e2e.rs` had not COMPILED since `sync_verbs` moved under
`profile`, and every gate in this repo was green throughout.

FIXED: `gate-rust-test-targets` in `before-push` runs `cargo check --all-targets`. Proven to
bite — reverting the one-line repair fails the gate.

`check`, NOT `clippy -D warnings`, and the distinction is the point. Clippy over test
targets turns years of style debt in fixtures into a red gate on arrival: its first run here
reported doc-comment formatting and a `MutexGuard` held across an await, none of which is
the failure this exists to catch. A gate red on arrival is a gate an operator learns to
bypass; this one asks a precise question instead — does it still compile.

STILL OPEN: the same blind spot exists for `packages/agent`, and the gate covers only
`packages/tractor`. Widening it is a line of config; what is worth measuring first is
whether the agent crate has integration tests at all.

issues.title: A peer id was keyed on the namespace STRING, so every in-memory sync wrote to the ambient graph base
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-18, and the shape is worth more than the fix.

`peer_id_for_namespace` returned `None` — no persistent home — for the literal namespace
`:memory:`, and read-or-created `{namespace}.peer` under the declared graph base for every
other name. A sync over IN-MEMORY storage built as `NativeSync::new(storage, "test")`
therefore wrote a file to disk.

Harmless while the base fell back to the process CWD. Once the base honoured the node's
declaration (ISS-123 — correctly), roughly fifteen test files became env-sensitive at once:
a sibling pointing REFARM_HOME at a TempDir that had since dropped failed whichever test ran
next. Roughly one run in three, with A DIFFERENT NAME EACH TIME.

## Three fixes before one

A per-test `env_lock` deflaked one test and the failure moved to the next. Locking fourteen
in that file moved it to another file. A lock inside a shared helper moved it again.

THE DIFFERENT NAME EACH RUN WAS THE EVIDENCE and I read it late: a failure that changes
identity between runs is not several bugs, it is one cause with several victims. Every lock
was a second door into one rule.

## The rule, stated once

A peer id is the identity of a PERSISTED replica. Storage that does not survive the process
has none, whatever its namespace is called — and derivation from the namespace already keeps
in-process replicas distinct without a file. `NativeStorage` now carries whether it is
persistent, and that fact decides, not a name.

Thirteen of fourteen consecutive full-suite runs green after, against roughly two in three
before. The scattered guards were removed rather than kept: leaving them would say the cure
was the lock.

WORTH WATCHING: prior art in a90028cb deflaked two env tests before this slice, so a residual
env-race class predates it. If a name recurs, it is that class and not this rule.

issues.title: A node declares the tools it depends on but does not ship
issues.body:
A node runs on tools it did not build (gh, rsync, cargo, a VPN client). Nothing measured them: a presence check passes for a gh from 2022, and the staleness only surfaces as an unrelated subcommand failing mid-work. Measured on the operator's node as 'gh version 2.4.0+dfsg1 (2022-03-23)'.

SHIPPED: packages/health/src/tool-requirements.js — pure, four states (ok / absent / outdated / cannot-say), malformed entries reported rather than dropped. Wired through ToolchainAuditor (which already existed, was generic, and had NO consumer outside its own test) into refarm health, which reports results.nodeTools and recommends per state with no invented fix command.

THREE THINGS THE SLICE CLOSED BEYOND THE FEATURE:
1. Privilege boundary. Auditing a tool RUNS it, so the declaration is read from the NODE tier only. auditConfigTier is reporting-only today, so readNodeToolDeclaration enforces it at the reader itself; a workspace config declaring nodeTools is refused AND reported. Registered in CONFIG_KEY_OWNERSHIP and docs/CONFIG_TIERS.md.
2. Cache staleness. The health audit cache fingerprints the REPOSITORY; a node tool is outside that tree, so no hash of it notices gh being upgraded. Tool checks are re-measured on every run including cache hits, and the report is rebuilt rather than patched.
3. Regression from 772480bd. packages/config's suite had been red since the Copilot dispatch adapter landed: github-copilot gained a runtime adapter and the test still asserted it had none. Fixed; 147/147.

Docs: docs/node-tools.md. Step toward describing the node rather than copying it.

issues.title: The lane's per-step budget is below the cold cost of the package it validates
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-18, three times. "refarm agent finish --lane after-edit --run" reported FAIL on package-apps-refarm-validation with elapsedMs=180106 against FINISH_PROCESS_TIMEOUT_MS=180000 (agent-finish-plan.ts:44). No test failed: the step was KILLED at the ceiling. The other three steps of the lane finish in under 3 seconds combined.

THE FIRST DIAGNOSIS WAS "cold turbo cache" AND IT WAS TOO COARSE. Measured directly: a run with 78 of 79 tasks ALREADY CACHED still took 2m6s. One uncached task — "test" — is ~126s on its own, 70% of the whole budget. The real rule is narrower and worse: the step fits in 180s only when the TEST task itself is cached, and any source edit to apps/refarm or to a package it depends on invalidates exactly that task. That is most slices. Warming the cache outside the ceiling then makes the step finish in 721ms — a workaround, because the gate passes only because the work already happened where the gate could not see it.

THE MISREPORT IS FIXED (2026-08-18). commandPlanSpawnErrorMessage returned stderr whenever it was non-empty and only produced its timeout sentence when stderr was EMPTY — so a process that printed anything before being killed (turbo's startup banner is enough) reported the banner and nothing else. The one fact that explained the result was the one fact suppressed.

Now: CommandPlanStepRunResult carries `timedOut` and `timeoutMs`; the run-level status has a third value `timed-out` beside `passed`/`failed`; the message names the kill FIRST and keeps the partial output as evidence; the resume record and summary carry the outcome, so `refarm resume` says "killed at its time ceiling" instead of "complete the failed validation handoff". A widened predicate keeps a killed gate's recovery commands, which the naive split would have silently dropped.

THREE ANSWERS REMAIN OPEN, and they are the operator's to choose:
1. Raise FINISH_PROCESS_TIMEOUT_MS above the cold cost of the largest package.
2. Split `test` out of the validation step so the other three tasks are not held hostage to it.
3. Warm the cache as part of the lane, before the timed step.

None of the three is done. What is done is that choosing between them no longer requires first discovering that nothing was broken.

issues.title: nodeTools is declared through the guided path, not by hand
issues.body:
ISS-148 shipped the reader and stopped at "writing the config is the operator's call". That was the wrong stopping point: this repository already has the blocks for exactly this, and leaving the operator to hand-edit JSON is the failure mode the blocks exist to prevent.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO ISS-148:
1. SHAPE. nodeTools was an ARRAY. planCatalogDeclaration REFUSES a block that is not a record, so an array was a declaration no guided command could ever write — a fresh instance of the built-and-never-wired pattern. It is now a catalog block keyed by command, the same shape delivery/connections/surfaces/workspaces use. The key being the command also settles what two entries naming one binary mean: they cannot exist.
2. PATH. health.ts hardcoded ".refarm" while the new reader used sovereignConfigRelativePath. Two readers disagreeing about which file is the node config. Both now resolve through the same helper.

SHIPPED: "refarm tools add <command>" and "refarm tools list", composing prompt-contract-v1 (channel-abstract), operation-consent-v1 (whole-file diff, durable record, undo) and catalog-authoring (keyed write preserving unowned fields, ISS-036). Nothing re-implemented. The only thing tools.ts owns is measuring the binary BEFORE asking, so the floor the operator authorises is a number they were shown — the line between a draft accepted and an inference nobody decided.

ATTENDED HALF PROVEN LIVE 2026-08-18 against the node at 127.0.0.1:42001. "tools add --attended-elsewhere" published the journey to the pending-prompt hub; GET /prompts showed the consent select with all three options and the measurement in the notices; POST /prompts/{id}/answer with "authorize" from an external client woke the command, which returned status authorized and wrote the declaration with an undo record. The terminal was never used for the decision. Same pending-prompt.v1 wire an attending PWA reads — curl stood in for the device, not for the protocol. Two regression tests hold the wiring: the flag must select the attended channel, and no publisher must yield the same "deferred" as a headless terminal.

THREE ARCHITECTURAL GUARDS CAUGHT SHORTCUTS, and each pointed somewhere better:
- process-boundary refused node:child_process in app source, which moved measureTool into @refarm.dev/health beside the auditor that already spawns.
- ancestor-option refused --args (collides with Commander's positional bag) and then --version-args (variadic, invisible to the guard's probe — see ISS-151). The flag became one token, which also removed speculative generality: a version probe is one token in practice.
- probe-coverage required "tools list" to be accounted for; it is now registered in the directory-independence probe with its reason.

REFUSALS THAT ARE THE POINT: a tool that did not run is refused rather than declared (--even-if-absent says it out loud); the consent notes state that authorising the declaration ALSO authorises an execution, because health runs the binary on every audit; with no operator nothing is written.

issues.title: The ancestor-option guard calls a variadic option swallowed when it is not
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-18 while adding "refarm tools add". The ancestor-option guard probes a value-taking option by declaring it with a sentinel and asserting opts()[attribute] === MIRROR_VALUE. A VARIADIC option ("--x <args...>") receives [MIRROR_VALUE] — an array — so the equality fails and the guard reports landedOn "(nowhere)": the exact wording it uses for an option the operator's flag never reaches.

The report is therefore wrong in a specific, expensive way. It does not say "this guard cannot model variadic options"; it says the flag is swallowed and tells the author to read it with optsWithGlobals(), which will not help because nothing was wrong. The first author to hit this spends the debugging on their own command.

NOBODY IN apps/refarm DECLARES A VARIADIC OPTION TODAY. That is why this has never fired, and it is also why fixing the guard now has no caller to validate against — which is the argument for recording it rather than changing a shared architectural guard for a hypothetical.

The slice that found it dropped its variadic flag for an unrelated and better reason (a version probe is one token in practice), so nothing is blocked. What is left is the guard's blind spot and its misleading message.

TWO HONEST FIXES when someone needs one: teach the probe to accept [MIRROR_VALUE] for variadic options, or make the message distinguish "never arrived" from "arrived in a shape this guard does not model". The second is cheaper and removes the wrong diagnosis, which is the part that costs.

issues.title: The allowance is a conditional promise, and nothing shows when the condition failed
issues.body:
`workspaceAllowances` bounds what this node dispatches for a workspace in a UTC calendar month, and refuses before spending (01b3d991). Two questions it does NOT answer are the operator's, and both get harder to change the longer they wait.

1. WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE COUNT IS IMPOSSIBLE.

The gate has three outcomes. `cannot-check` -- the record could not be read -- PERMITS and says so on stderr. That choice was made here, not by the operator: a node that refuses work because it cannot count is unusable exactly when its runtime is down.

The consequence is that the allowance is a CONDITIONAL promise: it holds while the record is readable. A month of silent `cannot-check` is indistinguishable, from the outside, from a month spent inside the allowance -- and that is the only way this design can mislead.

If a hard guarantee is wanted instead ("never exceed, whatever happens"), the choice inverts and a read failure becomes paralysis. Neither is free.

WHAT WOULD MAKE THE CURRENT CHOICE SAFE: `cannot-check` has to land somewhere the operator looks LATER, not only on the stderr of the moment. Today it scrolls past. That is the concrete next piece of work either way, because it is what turns a conditional promise into a visible one.

2. WHERE THE ALLOWANCE LIVES.

It is a node-tier config key today, which is right by the tier rules -- deciding what may be spent is the node's business. The consequence appears with the second node: the allowance does NOT travel with the workspace.

  Node fact:      "this machine lets no workspace spend more than X." Protects the seat of whoever operates the machine. What is built.
  Workspace fact: "this work has this budget, wherever it runs." Follows the workspace between nodes, so the same work is capped identically on the PC and on the phone.

The mesh -> PWA -> x86-node ladder makes the second reading matter. Nothing needs deciding before the first allowance is declared; it needs deciding before allowances are declared on SEVERAL workspaces, because migrating afterwards means reconciling two sources of truth.

issues.title: A Rust lib test flaked once and the run that saw it hid which one
issues.body:
OBSERVED 2026-08-19, once in roughly seven runs of `cargo test --lib` on packages/tractor: 1503 passed, 1 failed. Five consecutive re-runs afterwards were clean, and the failure did not reproduce.

THE NAME IS UNKNOWN, AND THAT IS THE PART WORTH FIXING. The run used `--quiet`, which prints the result line and suppresses the `failures:` block naming which test failed. So a real intermittent failure was observed and cannot be chased, because the only invocation that saw it threw away the one fact needed to act on it.

That is the same shape as ISS-149's timeout envelope: the output that reports a problem omits the field that identifies it. The cheap fix is at the invocation, not in any test — a run that reports a failure must name it.

WHAT WAS RULED OUT by measurement rather than assumption: it is not the live daemon. Five clean runs happened with the node's `tractor` process up and holding its databases, which was the first hypothesis.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN: which test, and whether it is order- or parallelism-dependent. `cargo test` runs the lib suite in one process with threads, and this repository has fixed exactly that class before (the peer-id flake, resolved by keying identity on persistence rather than on name).

NOT INVESTIGATED FURTHER on purpose: chasing an unnamed flake by re-running is how an afternoon disappears. Recorded so the next observer starts with "run it without --quiet" instead of with five more runs.

issues.title: The node executes the development repo, and nothing says so
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-19. The node's supervised services execute the development repo's build output:

  systemd unit  ->  ~/.local/bin/refarm (313-byte shim)  ->  ~/github/refarm/apps/refarm/dist/index.js

Consequences: a build rewrites what live services run; a branch switch changes them silently; `backup create` carries 32 files and none is code; and declaring the runtime as a supervised process would encode a repo path into a unit.

## SHIPPED: the node says it (745717da, 2cefdd69, c928117e)

`refarm health` reports `nodeSubstrate` under "Worth knowing" -- `severity: info`, so it never leads a handoff and never reddens the gate. The backup manifest carries `substrate: { kind, executes, repository, included: false }` beside `secrets.included`. Documented with a diagram in `docs/NODE_SUBSTRATE.md`, cross-referenced from `SANDBOX_NODE.md`.

## SHIPPED: the install path is OPEN (9c43fac9, 129b3d26, 305e9827)

An earlier revision of this item called separation a packaging project. That was asserted from a quick read and was WRONG. Measured, then fixed:

  node <deploy>/dist/index.js --version        -> 0.1.0
  node <deploy>/dist/index.js model providers  -> answers

Run from /tmp with the repository nowhere on the path. 465MB, self-contained, built by `pnpm --filter @refarm.dev/refarm deploy --prod --legacy`.

THREE DEFECTS STOOD IN THE WAY, one family -- the manifest not declaring what the code needs:

1. `files` ENUMERATED individual paths in 5 packages (root, windmill, health, cli, config), so every file added later had to be remembered. Three of the unshipped files were written earlier the same session, unknowingly.
2. `plugin-manifest` shipped a `dist` containing ZERO .js files while its `exports` named `./src/index.js`. Not merely the last mile: installed from a registry it failed on first import, and had done so invisibly for as long as everything resolved through the workspace. Protected surface; touched with explicit operator authorisation.
3. `infra-cloudflare` resolved `wrangler` -- a devDependency -- at MODULE LOAD, so an optional capability made its dependency mandatory on every node. Now resolved lazily, with a refusal that names the decision rather than the resolver's file.

`scripts/ci/package-files-closure-gate.mjs` walks the transitive closure from every published entry point and reports EVERY offender. 142 packages whole.

This was simultaneously the 0.1.0 release's own rope, measured as SHIPPED-dist rather than built-dist.

## WHAT REMAINS, and it is the operator's

The pieces exist; nothing yet PROMOTES. A `refarm node install` would assemble the tree, verify it by RUNNING it, repoint the shim, and keep the previous version for rollback. Each of those is now a known-reachable step rather than a project, and the verification step is the one that matters: an install that reports success without running what it installed is the shape of backup that fails on the day it is needed.

Until then the coupling stands, declared. The node says what it runs; the manifest says the bundle does not carry it.

## THE SEPARATION WAS NOT ACHIEVED, and this item said it was (55ce220e)

MEASURED 2026-08-22. `pnpm deploy` HARDLINKS workspace packages, so the assembled tree shared inodes with `packages/<pkg>/dist` -- 29 of 29 sampled. Everything above was true and the node was still executing the working tree; the launcher said the opposite, in a comment, in the file.

  20/08 00:58  `tsc` rewrote index.js IN PLACE. Same inode -> the installed copy changed too.
  20/08 01:15  the same commit added bindings.ts. A NEW file; hardlinks are per-file, so it never arrived.
  21/08 09:18  reboot. Every unit reloaded from disk and died. web-serve gave up after six restarts.
  22/08 20:25  found. credential-renew had failed 4420 times in between, silently.

`readNodeSubstrate` could not see it: it classifies by asking whether a `.git` sits above the entrypoint, and `~/.local/lib/refarm/...` has none -- so it answered `installed` and had nothing to say.

NO FLAG PREVENTS IT. `--config.package-import-method=copy`, its environment form, and `--config.inject-workspace-packages=true` were each measured hardlinking anyway. Independence is now TAKEN after assembly, between assembling and verifying, and PROVEN against the checkout by inode rather than by the materialiser's own selection -- the first version of that proof reused the selection, misread pnpm's peer suffix, and reported independence with 1081 files still shared.

Verified on the node: 16552 files, 0 shared, measured independently of the install that made it.

issues.title: pnpm deploy --legacy leaves the source checkout unable to run its own gates
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-19, reproducible in four steps from a clean checkout:

  pnpm install                                       -> "Already up to date" (~2s)
  pnpm exec node -e '...'                            -> runs
  pnpm --filter <pkg> deploy --prod --legacy <dir>   -> exit 0
  pnpm exec node -e '...'                            -> ERR_PNPM_ABORTED_REMOVE_MODULES_DIR_NO_TTY

`--legacy` runs its own `pnpm install --production`, and the workspace's recorded dependency status does not survive it. Afterwards EVERY `pnpm run` and `pnpm exec` in that checkout aborts -- `pnpm run build` and the repo's own quality lanes included. `pnpm install` (~2s, "Already up to date") puts it back, so nothing is actually stale; only the recorded status is.

`--legacy` is not optional: without it pnpm refuses with ERR_PNPM_DEPLOY_NONINJECTED_WORKSPACE unless the whole workspace sets `inject-workspace-packages=true` -- a 153-project layout change, not a slice.

## HANDLED where it is caused

`refarm node install` resyncs immediately after assembling, using the same resolved binary that made the mess, and BEFORE verification -- so even a failed verify leaves a working checkout. It reports a fourth state rather than assuming: `checkout: restored | stale`. The coupling is documented on `packageWorkspaceDeployCommand` in `@refarm.dev/config`.

## AUDIT OF OTHER CALLERS: done, and there are none

Searched `--legacy`, `pnpm deploy` and `"deploy"` across ts/js/mjs/json/yml/yaml/sh, excluding node_modules and dist:

  packages/config/src/package-manager.js     the resolver itself -- the only invoker
  scripts/ci/package-files-closure-gate.mjs  mentions it in a header comment; static analysis, spawns nothing
  apps/refarm/src/commands/deploy.ts         `refarm deploy` (targets) -- a different command that shares the word
  .github/workflows/**                       no match

So the footgun has exactly one caller and it is handled. What remained was not a second caller but the absence of an instrument.

## THE REAL GAP, and what closes it

No gate noticed. Measured on the poisoned checkout:

  refarm health --json          -> ok: true, issueCount: 0
  refarm check --next-action    -> ok: true, nextAction: null   <- the "all clear" the agent loop follows
  pnpm exec <anything>          -> aborts

Everything the repo knew about a workspace's executor was READ FROM FILES -- `workspace execution` reported `available: true` for both adapters on that checkout. Declared is not runnable.

CLOSED BY: `measureWorkspaceTooling` in `@refarm.dev/health`, which asks the manager to actually run something in the workspace and reports three states (`ready` / `broken` / `cannot-check`). Counted in `issueCount` -- broken NOW against something the workspace DECLARED, the same rule `nodeTools` follows -- so `check --next-action` now answers "Run `pnpm install` in that workspace." Costs one manager invocation: health goes from ~0.46s to ~0.93s, measured.

Never-installed is deliberately NOT broken: a manifest with no `node_modules` beside it is a workspace nobody set up, and claiming its tooling "stopped working" would fire on every scratch directory holding a package.json.

ALSO FOUND while wiring it: the health audit cache fingerprints the REPOSITORY, and a poisoned checkout changes no tracked file -- so a cached "all clear" returned forever. `nodeTools` and `credentialRenewal` already had hand-written re-measurements on the cache-hit branch for exactly this reason, and the third one was briefly added to only one of the two branches. All four machine facts now live in a single `measureMachineFacts`, which also fixed a latent one: `nodeSubstrate` was NOT re-measured on a cache hit, so after `refarm node install` repointed the launcher a cached health still reported the old substrate.

Standing lesson: the failure was invisible to 3699 passing tests plus every architecture guard. Guards prove WHERE execution goes, not WHETHER it works.

issues.title: The ancestor-option floor asserts a wall-clock budget inside a parallel suite
issues.body:
SEEN 2026-08-19. `apps/refarm` full run: 1 failed | 3691 passed. Failing test:

  test/architecture/ancestor-option-conformance.test.ts
  > "saw the options it claims to have audited -- the audit is not vacuous"

Ran green in isolation (88/88) and green on the next full run (3692/3692). Unlike ISS-153, the cause is legible from the source rather than unknown.

## Why it can flake

That test asserts `expect(timedOut).toEqual([])` over every probed command, and `timedOut` is filled by a WALL-CLOCK budget: `PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS = 4_000`, raced against `parseAsync`. The probes run inside a 249-file suite with parallel workers, so a command that normally settles in milliseconds can lose 4s of wall clock to scheduling pressure alone -- no defect in the command, no defect in the harness's logic.

The other two floors in the same test (`OBSERVED.size` and `withReads.length`) are counts, not clocks, and cannot flake this way.

## Why it matters more than a normal flake

This harness exists to prevent a FOURTH instance of an operator's flag never arriving. A floor that fails for load reasons trains its readers to re-run rather than read it, which is how the real signal gets waved past -- the same argument `operation-consent-v1` makes about a prompt nobody learns from.

## Not yet decided

Whether a timeout should fail the audit at all, or be reported the way the file already reports its other gaps (printed, named, counted, not asserted). It is currently the only clock-based assertion in a file that is otherwise careful to measure rather than assume.

issues.title: A quota refusal names neither the exhausted meter nor the idle seat beside it
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-20, while proving ISS-140 end to end on the operator's node.

    refarm credential quota
      pessoal      individual  premium_interactions  1500/1500   chat unlimited  completions unlimited
      corporativo  business    premium_interactions     0/10000  chat unlimited  completions unlimited
      openai-codex             cannot-ask

    refarm ask --workspace refarm 'responda apenas: ok'     (bound to corporativo)
      -> "Model quota or billing limit reached.
          Inspect route:     refarm model current
          Reconfigure/login: refarm sow
          List providers:    refarm model providers"

Every suggested next step is about the ROUTE. Not one of them is the situation. The node had
already read, and could have said:

  - WHICH METER. `premium_interactions`, not the seat. `chat` and `completions` are UNLIMITED on
    that same seat, so "quota reached" is false as a statement about the account.
  - THE NUMBERS AND THE DATE. 0 of 10000, resets 2026-09-01. An operator reading "limit reached"
    cannot tell a seat that is finished for the month from one that is finished forever.
  - THAT ANOTHER AUTHORISED SEAT HAS ROOM. 1500 idle premium interactions sitting on the personal
    seat, invisible at the only moment they matter.

## Why this is the sustainability axis and not a message tweak

The node's cost work assumes capacity is FUNGIBLE ACROSS AUTHORISED SEATS -- that is what
`workspaceAllowances`, `budget by-account` and the per-account quota reader are for. A refusal
that names neither the exhausted meter nor the idle one makes that capacity unreachable exactly
when it is needed, so the accounting describes a fleet the operator cannot actually steer.

## What must NOT be built

AUTOMATIC FAILOVER. The personal/corporate frontier is the operator's, and a node that silently
spends a personal seat for corporate work has crossed it without being asked. The same reasoning
`credential quota` already follows for its third state applies: say exactly what is known, leave
the decision where it belongs. The gap is INFORMATION, not policy.

Nor a second quota reader: `credential quota` already extracts all of this. What is missing is
that the refusal path does not consult it.

## Open questions for the operator, framed by long-term cost

1. Should the refusal offer a COMMAND that switches the binding (`refarm credential bind`), or
   only state the facts? Offering it makes the crossing one keystroke, which is either the point
   or exactly the wrong thing depending on how strict the frontier is.
2. Should a workspace be able to declare more than one authorised seat in priority order, so the
   operator states the crossing ONCE rather than at each refusal? That is the declarative answer
   and it is bigger; it also composes with `workspaceAllowances`, which already reasons per month.

## Also seen, smaller

`refarm budget by-account` groups by opaque credential id with `label: null`. The alias is known
(`pessoal`, `corporativo`) and does not reach the grouping, so the one surface built to show where
money went reads as two ULIDs.

## TIER 1 LANDED 2026-08-20 — the declaration, and the walk that honours it.

Question 2 above was the operator's choice: a workspace declares its seats in priority order, so
the personal/corporate crossing is stated ONCE rather than decided at every refusal.

    credential bind <workspace> <id> [<id>...]     the order IS the instruction
    resolveModelAccount                            walks it; never reorders it
    ask                                            falls to the next DECLARED seat on a quota
                                                   refusal, and only on one

WALKED ON A FACT, NOT A PREDICTION, and this is the load-bearing choice. Reading quota and
skipping exhausted seats needs to know which METER a model consumes, and no such map exists: the
corporate seat is 0/10000 on premium_interactions and UNLIMITED on chat and completions, so a
predictive skip would cross the frontier for nothing. A provider refusing the seat is evidence.

FOUR PROPERTIES, each against a specific way of being wrong:
  - only on quota (walking on any error spends a second seat on a bug, twice)
  - only before any text reached the operator (a spliced answer is worse than a refusal)
  - the declared list is EXCLUSIVE (exhausted, it refuses; it never falls to an unnamed seat)
  - one provider per order, refused at WRITE time (a fallback that changes provider changes the
    route, which is resolved before the effort is submitted)

PROVEN LIVE, then reverted. `refarm` declared [corporativo, pessoal]; the dispatch that had
refused now answers, and the record is falsifiable:

    corporativo   17 -> 18 observations,  7309 ->  7309 tokens   (attempted, spent nothing)
    pessoal       20 -> 21 observations, 29431 -> 31584 tokens   (paid, +2153)

The attempt is recorded against the seat that refused and the spend against the seat that paid, so
a walk is visible in `budget by-account` rather than hidden inside one row.

The declaration was REVERTED afterwards: which order to declare is a crossing of the operator's own
personal/corporate frontier, and the feature exists so that HE writes it.

## STILL OPEN

QUESTION 1 above, untouched: the refusal still says "Model quota or billing limit reached" and
names neither the exhausted meter, its numbers and reset date, nor the idle capacity beside it.
With a declared order the walk now handles the common case silently, which makes the message
matter LESS at dispatch and MORE everywhere else — `credential quota` is the only surface that
answers it, and nothing routes an operator there at the moment he needs it.

AND THE ROUTER, recorded as a study case at the operator's request: GitHub Copilot's `auto` mode
picks a MODEL underneath; the analogous axis here is picking a SEAT. The base is deliberately shaped
so a router could only ever choose WITHIN the declared order — the same monotonic property the host
enforces on routes (narrowing only, never widening). It would remain opt-in by operator intent.

issues.title: The installed tree's label names a commit it does not contain
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-22, immediately after ISS-154's coupling was closed.

`refarm node install` labels the assembled tree `<version>-<git HEAD>` but assembles it from the working tree's `dist/`. When the checkout is dirty, the label names a commit that does not contain the code in the tree.

Reproduced on the operator's node:

  installed 0.1.0-c58ae2ba carries materializeWorkspacePackages  -> yes
  git show c58ae2ba:apps/refarm/src/commands/node-install.ts     -> no such symbol

`installVersionLabel`'s own docstring states the purpose: "two installs of 0.1.0 from different commits are different trees, and an operator rolling back has to tell them apart in a directory listing". It cannot: two trees labelled c58ae2ba may differ by whatever was uncommitted at each install.

This blocks the INTENTIONAL UPDATE CYCLE the operator asked for (2026-08-22): deciding to update a node on purpose needs a label that says what the node actually runs. A label that is nearly-but-not-quite traceable is worse than none, because it invites the trust it cannot carry.

Candidate shapes, undecided: refuse to install from a dirty checkout; or mark the label (`c58ae2ba-dirty`); or record a content digest of the assembled tree beside the label. The third also serves ISS-159.

issues.title: Nothing compares what the node RUNS with what the checkout HAS
issues.body:
MEASURED 2026-08-22. `readNodeSubstrate` answers `installed` and `describeSubstrate` returns null — deliberately, because an installed substrate was the goal state and had nothing to explain.

But an installed node AGES, and nothing says by how much. The node ran 0.1.0-5b4810a9 while the checkout moved 10 commits past it, and no surface said so. Ageing is legitimate; being silent about it is not.

The operator's requirement, in his own words (2026-08-22): the node must not be coupled to the repo, and the update cycle must be INTENTIONAL — 'seja via oficial quando publicado ou nesse nosso desenvolvimento local'. An intentional cycle needs a trigger, and the trigger is a comparison that does not exist: which build does this node execute, and is it behind what I have?

Shape, undecided: the installed tree records its identity (label, commit, digest) at install; `readNodeSubstrate` reads it back; `refarm health`/`resume` state it, and say the distance from the checkout's HEAD without grading it as a defect — the same posture ISS-154 chose for the working-tree substrate (info, never reddening the gate).

Depends on ISS-158: a label that names a commit it does not contain cannot anchor the comparison.
